title: Israeli ex-generals urge Trump to push Netanyahu on ‘settler terror’
excerpt:
Netanyahu heads to Washington as Israeli ex-officials urge Trump to curb West Bank violence

Hundreds of former Israeli military, diplomatic, and intelligence officials are asking United States Presid...
body_text:
Netanyahu heads to Washington as Israeli ex-officials urge Trump to curb West Bank violence

Hundreds of former Israeli military, diplomatic, and intelligence officials are asking United States President Donald Trump to urge Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to curb “settler terror” in the occupied West Bank.

In a letter published on Tuesday, the nearly 600 former officials appealed to Trump, saying he was the only one capable of helping to avoid the “calamity” of escalating violence in the West Bank and its implications for Israeli, US, and regional security.

“Unless arrested swiftly and decisively, escalating violence in the West Bank is poised to ignite the region and carries severe ramifications for both Israeli security and U.S. regional interests,” the letter, written by lobby group Commanders for Israel’s Security (CIS), said.

“It is our professional judgment that no one but you, Mr. President, can avert this calamity,” it said.

CIS is a Zionist movement of more than 550 retired Israeli army colonels and generals, as well as equivalent ranks in Mossad, Shin Bet, Israeli Police, the foreign service, and other corps.

The group’s stated mission is “securing Israel’s future as the strong democratic home of the Jewish people”.

CIS also wrote that it is “no secret” that certain government members “orchestrate much of this chaos”, including by protecting settlers and Israeli forces from the scrutiny of the law.

The “swell in Jewish settler terror activity” risks consequences that may prove even more catastrophic than the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel and its multi-front fallout, the group said.

The group called on Trump to raise the issue with Netanyahu in their meeting in Washington, DC, on Tuesday.

The letter comes after widespread pogroms and violence by Israeli settlers across the occupied West Bank over the weekend following a deadly shootout in the town of Tal in which two Israelis and four Palestinians were killed.

Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh said the letter aligns with other warnings from the Israeli defence establishment against Israeli settlers “taking on the initiative” and “calling the shots” on behalf of the Israeli army, and “putting even Israeli soldiers in harm’s way”.

Netanyahu is due to meet Trump on Tuesday in his seventh trip to the White House during Trump’s second term.

His trip comes as the latest escalation in fighting between Iran and the US is paused to give space for diplomatic efforts.

title: ‘We have lost everything’: extreme rainfall across Asia brings flash floods and typhoons
excerpt:
From Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdown

“It rained for 10 days and 10 nights, non-stop – I’d never seen anything like it,” says Anar Gul, a...
body_text:
From Afghanistan to Taiwan, unprecedented deluge highlights devastating impact of climate breakdown

“It rained for 10 days and 10 nights, non-stop – I’d never seen anything like it,” says Anar Gul, a construction worker who lives in the remote district of Dur Baba in eastern Afghanistan.

The houses in his village are built from stone and mud, which makes them extremely vulnerable to heavy rains. After days of rain, Gul’s kitchen collapsed and his neighbour, Sayed Afsar Sadat, saw a large part of his house completely destroyed. “Rains like this are coming heavier and earlier each year,” says Sadat. “They are destroying the roads and washing away our crops. It’s impacting us directly.”

Last week, torrential rains and flash floods wiped out villages and towns in Afghanistan, leaving at least 31 people dead and hundreds missing. It’s been a similar picture in neighbouring countries, with the monsoon rains sparking chaos across the region. India, Bangladesh and Pakistan have all seen erratic, sudden heavy dumps of water.

Jesmin Akter lived in the city of Chattogram, on the south-eastern coast of Bangladesh, which received a record 412.3mm of rainfall in 24 hours in early July, leading to the flash flood that swept through the Banshkhali district where they live. She says her children “understand that we are in a very bad situation”.

Overnight the rains took the little they had; their poultry died, their paddy field flooded, their house collapsed and all their belongings in it – children’s books, school bags, toys, clothes, kitchen items – ruined.

Akter carried her six children through chest-deep water to her mother’s house. There they stayed in the crowded conditions for over a week until the water receded.

“We have lost everything,” Akter said. Their house beside the canal was not in a good condition, but a few months ago the family had repaired it. “Now the flood has destroyed it again. We have no money. We are surviving on the food assistance we receive from different organisations.” They have gone back to the ruins of their home, but her children sleep on plastic sheets laid on the wet floor and she worries for their safety, especially that the unsanitary conditions will lead to disease. Her daughter has developed a fever.

As wildfires rage across Europe and North America, the unprecedented rains continue elsewhere. While South Korea swings between heatwave and downpour, in Japan and Vietnam torrential rain has led to landslides. China, meanwhile, has seen bouts of extreme rainfall since the flood season began in April, according to the water resources ministry in mid-July, marking the start of a month-long peak flood control window. More than 600 rivers have since risen above warning levels – a 35% jump from the average for the same period over the past five years.

In the south-western city of Chongqing, a huge landslide after torrential rain killed at least 11 people and left 50 missing, with rescue efforts still ongoing. Separately, a flash flood at a scenic camping spot in the north-central province of Gansu left 10 people dead and injured 23 others.

The flood season across the region has been exacerbated by successive storms. Typhoon Noul, the strongest to make landfall in China so far this year, prompted the evacuation of more than 890,000 people in Guangdong as of Sunday evening, according to provincial authorities. In early July, Typhoon Maysak inundated parts of Guangxi and swept through commercial snake farms, allowing hundreds of snakes to escape.

Forecasters have warned that more wet weather is on the way. Much of northern China, including Beijing, is expected to receive 20% to 50% more rain than usual, while four to six typhoons are forecast to make landfall in or affect the country this summer, above the average of 4.2, according to the China Meteorological Administration.

Taiwan, an island that lies in the path of typhoons in the north-west Pacific, has also seen a rise in extreme rainfall. In June, repeated downpours caused more than NT$330m (about US$10.2m) in agricultural losses across Taiwan, according to the agriculture ministry, while the capital Taipei recorded its highest monthly rainfall in more than a century.

The extreme weather across the region can clearly be linked to climate change. Climate scientists have long predicted that large areas of Asia will disproportionately suffer from more intense heat, humidity and drought as a result of climate disruption caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal. The most recent report by the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change said rising temperatures raise the threat of “floods in monsoon regions in south, south-east and east Asia, and glacier melting in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region”.

And World Weather Attribution scientists have warned that extreme rainfall from cyclones is being “supercharged” in south-east Asia, with a clear pattern of increasingly heavy rain over recent decades.

The year 2025 saw devastating storms and rainfall across the region. It also saw ocean temperatures rise to record heights. So far, this year has brought record-breaking heatwaves. Extreme rainfall is more common and more intense because of human-caused climate breakdown across most of the world, particularly in Europe, most of Asia, central and eastern North America, and parts of South America, Africa and Australia. This is because warmer air can hold more water vapour and flooding has most likely become more frequent and severe in these locations as a result.

“More intense rainfall is an expected consequence of us heating the planet by burning fossil fuels and building up more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. A warmer atmosphere can carry more water, so when it rains, it rains harder. Also hotter conditions cause air to rise faster and drive more intense thunderstorms,” said Richard Betts, head of the climate impacts strategic area at the Met Office Hadley Centre.

The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) in providing aid helped the Guardian obtain interviews with those affected.

Dr Hosam Faysal, the head of IFRC’s country delegation in Afghanistan, said “these are the very real, humanitarian effects of a changing climate … becoming increasingly volatile”.

Faysal urged governments to ensure there was more investment in locally-led preparedness and mitigation in order to reduce the loss of life and suffering before climate-related disasters happened.

“The coming forecast El Niño is a clear example – waiting to respond to the extreme needs we can see coming only once they arrive will cost lives.”

title: A dog saved Houssein Hamze from a bomb. When war returned, he stayed to care for Lebanon’s animals
excerpt:
In normal times the Mashala shelter founder takes in strays, but in wartime, he is the only lifeline for animals in the area

During Israel’s 2006 war against Hezbollah, Houssein Hamze woke up one nig...
body_text:
In normal times the Mashala shelter founder takes in strays, but in wartime, he is the only lifeline for animals in the area

During Israel’s 2006 war against Hezbollah, Houssein Hamze woke up one night to the sound of barking. Alarmed, he got up to check on the dog – his first rescue pet. Moments later, a bomb dropped next to his home and a piece of shrapnel landed right where he had been sleeping.

“I swear to God, he really saved me from death. Animals always possess a sixth sense we don’t have,” Hamze said.

Twenty years and two wars later, the 57-year-old is still repaying his debt to the dog that saved his life.

Soon after his near-death experience, Hamze founded the Mashala shelter in the village of Zefta, south Lebanon, to take care of animals in the area. In normal times he takes in strays, and in wartime he is the only lifeline for animals in the area.

On a recent morning, Hamze strolled through his small farm where the shelter is located, checking on fig trees as a line of dogs followed behind him, ears perking up with his every move. He opened an enclosure where two camels – rescued from the Bekaa valley last year – stood among chickens and geese.

“This is Jamoola and her son, Jamool. She is so sweet. When I don’t visit for more than two days, she starts to cry. And when I come back, she wraps her neck around me as if she’s hugging me,” Hamze said, as the camel placed her head in his lap, nuzzling him as he scratched behind her ears. Jamool, a calf who was still nursing, hid his face behind his mother.

The donation-supported farm hosts an eclectic collection of rescues. About 200 dogs – some of them missing ears or tails – gnawed on donated chicken feet, while horses whinnied at guests by the entrance. Chickens ran between the camels’ legs while geese patrolled the perimeter of their enclosure. A small conspiracy of ravens flew rings around the forested valley of the farm, never straying too far from the shade in the intense summer heat.

Hamze was one of about 20 people who stayed behind in his village during the last Hezbollah-Israel war that started on 2 March 2026 and forced approximately a quarter of Lebanon’s population to flee their homes. He stayed to take care of the animals, despite the constant risk of death from Israeli drone and airstrikes.

“Many people fled and left their animals behind during their displacement – some of them left their animals tied up. We would go out, untie them and leave them water,” said Hamze. He pointed to one dog he rescued, Lulu, who lost a chunk of her tail in an airstrike and for whom he has been caring ever since. About 50 dogs came to the shelter during the war by themselves, seeking out food.

During the conflict, Hamze would make daily rounds in his beaten-up truck, distributing dry food to the abandoned dogs and livestock in the villages of south Lebanon. It was not easy work: food was hard to secure, and he would often have to carry jerrycans of water long distances to dogs in more remote areas. On several occasions, airstrikes hit a building next to where he was working. Once during his feeding rounds, Hamze stumbled on the corpse of a man recently struck by a drone strike.

“By the end, all the dogs knew me. I would beep and they would come running,” he said.

Hamze would travel between the villages despite a Israeli drone that hovered overhead, watching his every move. He stuck the “Mashala” animal shelter sign on the roof of the car so the drone could identify him – but still it was no sure bet. Drones would regularly strike people in the area, ranging from Hezbollah fighters to medics to a man and his friend who went back to collect clothes from their home.

“I wasn’t afraid for myself. I was only afraid for the animals. I kept thinking: if I die, who will look after them? They would be lost,” Hamze said.

Despite his bravado, Hamze quietly made arrangements in case he was killed. He sent eight donkeys to a shelter in Beirut, fearful that unlike the dogs, they would not be able to survive on their own if he died. He would have sent the camels and horses too, but he could not fit them in a pickup truck.

Since a ceasefire in June ended most of fighting in Lebanon, life has gone back to almost normal for Hamze and the animals in his shelter. The thud of artillery is more distant now; it no longer sets off a row of furious barking. Hamze is now occupied with more mundane tasks: repairing irrigation tubing chewed on by dogs, and chasing animals with a syringe to give them their tick treatments.

His work during the war made him a minor celebrity in Lebanon. Videos of him braving drones to feed dogs went viral, prompting an outpouring of donations. With the war no longer in the headlines, donations are slowly drying up.

Hamze is still famous in the village, though. His farm is hard to find but everyone in the area knows him. “Keep going all the way down the road and take a left. And tell Houssein I say hi,” said a shepherd on the road.

And there is more work than ever, Hamze said, as displaced people return to their homes and have begun calling him to assist with animal rescues. Scrolling through his WhatsApp, he estimated he received about 500 messages and calls a day reporting animals that needed help.

“The assistance is really not enough. But thank God, we made it through the most dangerous period. I was on my own, there wasn’t a single day when you could stop working and rest. I felt completely drained,” he said.

Hamze said he hoped that one day the shelter would not be necessary, that people would value animals as much as they do humans. Maybe, with a proper respect for the sanctity of life, people would stop fighting, he mused.

“The conclusion is this: if you don’t have compassion for animals, you won’t have compassion for human beings. Believe me,” Hamze said, before planting a kiss on Jamoola’s outstretched head.

title: Train drivers in Great Britain consider strike action over lack of toilets
excerpt:
Unions say basic needs still not being met a year after regulator told operators to improve facilities

Train drivers are considering strike action over a lack of toilets, with unions saying basic nee...
body_text:
Unions say basic needs still not being met a year after regulator told operators to improve facilities

Train drivers are considering strike action over a lack of toilets, with unions saying basic needs are still not addressed a year after the rail regulator told operators to provide more facilities and breaks.

Aslef said it was “putting the industry on notice”. The train drivers’ union added that companies had failed to deliver adequate toilets and reduce maximum driving times without a toilet break.

A 2024 report by Aslef from a survey of its members found widespread issues, with many drivers unable to reach working toilets and many resorting to urinating in bottles or defecating in the cabs.

The report said it had become a significant health and safety problem, with drivers left dehydrated because they were not drinking enough in order to avoid requiring a toilet break – putting passengers and staff at risk.

The union believed it had secured a breakthrough last summer when operators signed up to a charter set out by the rail safety board after a long campaign.

Richard Hines, HM chief inspector of railways at the Office of Rail and Road (ORR), wrote to train operators on 29 July 2025 telling them that “reliable welfare facilities [are] a basic requirement in any civilised society”. He said the current situation where some staff “lack adequate facilities or the time to use them, is unacceptable. This is a matter of human dignity, health, safety and respect to our people.”

Dave Calfe, the general secretary of Aslef, said: “We need action, not broken promises, to improve toilet facilities for drivers and to reduce the time drivers are expected to go without being able to take a toilet break. The health and wellbeing of our members is not a price we are prepared to pay for the inaction of the industry.”

The union said female drivers were particularly affected, and the situation was a deterrent to the railway’s attempts to recruit more women in the cab.

The welfare charter, which should have been implemented within 12 months, requires “safe, clean, accessible and dignified” toilets across the railway, and a maximum time of four hours in the driving seat without the chance to go to the toilet.

In the ORR’s annual report published this month, it said that despite the strong initial commitment and sign-up to the charter, “progress has been uneven and industry momentum has slowed. Key barriers remain, particularly around coordination, shared access to facilities, and consistent delivery.”

Conditions such as deep vein thrombosis, bladder issues, prostate cancer and colorectal cancer are believed to be linked to lack of toilet breaks.

Calfe said: “A year after train companies promised to do the right thing, drivers are still paying with their health for industry inaction. The industry and the government cannot continue failing the workforce on the most basic level, and we need action now.”

Strike action on the railway has been relatively limited since pay deals in 2024 ended almost two years of intermittent nationwide action at the end of the Covid pandemic. However, ballots are under way for drivers at LNER and Avanti; while RMT members at East Midlands railway will strike on 1 August over issues with its new trains.

The Unite union has also been campaigning for better toilets for bus drivers and lorry drivers, describing the lack of toilet facilities as a huge problem.

Wayne King, Unite’s national officer for passenger transport, said: “There are still nowhere enough toilets available for bus drivers. It’s the employer’s responsibility and they’re failing miserably. Drivers are using bottles as toilets, women are using she-pees with bottles. This has a dramatic impact on women during menstruation and menopause and members with underlying health conditions.

“During hot weather, drivers are not hydrating properly because they know there’s no toilets available on routes. This is a potential serious safety risk on multiple levels and can lead to the development of serious health conditions.”

Adrian Jones, Unite’s national officer for road transport, said: “Despite repeated promises by government and employers, there has been no real improvement in availability of toilets for lorry drivers.

“We need better access at delivery collection points, better and more roadside facilities and value for money at motorway service areas.”

A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “Train operators are legally required to provide suitable toilet facilities for their staff, and we expect them to meet these obligations.

“We strongly encourage industry to work together to ensure access to these facilities, and these kinds of welfare issues will be considered as we move towards Great British Railways.”

title: Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband details ‘big spiral’ as expert says one part ‘scared me’ in mom’s murder trial
excerpt:
Margaret McLean, a former prosecutor and Boston College law instructor, discussed Patrick Clancy’s testimony in his ex-wife’s murder trial.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, p...
body_text:
Margaret McLean, a former prosecutor and Boston College law instructor, discussed Patrick Clancy’s testimony in his ex-wife’s murder trial.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

Patrick Clancy, the father of three young children strangled inside their Massachusetts home, became the first witness Monday in his ex-wife’s murder trial, offering jurors a harrowing account of the mental health decline he witnessed before their deaths.

He was the first witness called in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, who faces murder charges in the deaths of the couple's three children in January 2023. Prosecutors argue she acted deliberately, while defense attorneys contend severe mental illness drove her actions.

Patrick described watching his then-wife fall into a "big spiral" after she began taking Seroquel, testifying that she lost weight, became severely depressed and began expressing suicidal thoughts.

"Awful," he said when asked how Lindsay was doing physically after starting the medication. "That was really where her big spiral started. She started to lose a lot of weight, and she became very depressed, and she was having a really hard time."

LINDSAY CLANCY’S HUSBAND COULD TESTIFY FOR HER AT TRIAL OVER DEATHS OF THEIR THREE CHILDREN

Patrick Clancy took the stand Monday and described watching his wife fall into a "big spiral" before she allegedly strangled their three young children inside the family’s Massachusetts home. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

Patrick also testified that Lindsay told him she was experiencing intrusive thoughts about harming their children, although she denied having a plan and said the thoughts disturbed her.

"I never saw Lindsay harm the kids," he told jurors.

Patrick Clancy exits Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., on Monday, July 27, 2026. His ex-wife, Lindsay Clancy, is on trial for the murder of their three children. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Margaret McLean, a former criminal prosecutor and trial attorney who teaches law at Boston College’s Carroll School of Management, said Patrick’s measured delivery did little to conceal the anguish of a father being forced to retrace the months preceding his children’s deaths.

"I think his demeanor on the stand is really quite clinical. He’s telling it as it is," McLean told Fox News Digital. "You can see the anguish within this man’s eyes, his facial expressions. You can tell he’s anguished up there, and it’s a horrible thing to have to relive and talk about."

McLean said Patrick appeared to be compartmentalizing his emotions as he listened carefully to the questions and provided straightforward answers.

"He’s got to get through this," she said. "He’s got to listen to the questions and provide the answers as best he can, and I think that he’s doing that."

Lindsay Clancy reacts as the details of her children's deaths are read in court on Monday. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL

Patrick testified that he was not concerned for the children’s safety when Lindsay first shared that the intrusive thoughts were telling her to hurt herself as well as her children. Moments after discussing the thoughts, he said, she could be seen making the children lunch, playing with them or preparing them for bed.

Patrick told jurors that he became alarmed after Lindsay was prescribed 13 psychiatric medications in the months prior to the murders and that he pushed for an in-person appointment because he believed there was a "disconnect" between the seriousness of her condition and the brief telehealth sessions she was receiving.

"It seemed like most of her telehealth appointments were pretty quick, and there just wasn’t, like, a lot of attention," he said.

Patrick also described taking Lindsay to hospital emergency departments and helping her enter McLean Hospital after she continued expressing suicidal thoughts.

He testified that he "would have paid anything" if insurance had become an obstacle to keeping her hospitalized.

Lindsay Clancy was indicted on three counts each of murder in the 2023 deaths of her 5-year-old daughter Cora, 3-year-old son Dawson and 7-month-old son Callan. She pleaded not guilty to the charges. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

The testimony could leave jurors asking whether the warning prompted an adequate response, McLean said, while cautioning against placing blame on Patrick or family members who may not have understood the severity of the risk.

"So many people don’t understand mental health today, so I’m not blaming him at all," McLean said. "Anybody might have done what he did, but that’s the part that scared me."

WATCH: Lindsay Clancy clutches tissues as jurors hear about her three children

Patrick’s testimony followed starkly different opening statements from prosecutors and the defense.

Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham told jurors that Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, were "deliberately and meticulously killed" by their mother on Jan. 24, 2023.

Buckingham alleged that Clancy deliberately sent Patrick from their Duxbury home to pick up medication and takeout food, giving herself enough time to strangle each child with an exercise band before attempting to kill herself.

McLean said Buckingham gave jurors a "roadmap of cold, calculated intent" while humanizing each child's interests and focusing on the time and physical effort required to carry out three separate strangulations.

"The prosecution did that because she [Buckingham] wants the jury to remember that the act of strangulation takes time and physical effort," McLean said. "It requires a conscious choice to continue three separate times."

Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham delivers her opening statement in court on Monday. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

The Commonwealth’s strategy, she said, is to reject the defense’s bid that Clancy suffered a sudden psychotic break and instead portray her as organized, purposeful and controlled.

During opening statements, defense attorney Kevin Reddington conceded that Clancy killed the children but argued that the only meaningful dispute is what was happening inside her mind.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

"She knows that she killed these children," Reddington told jurors. "The issue for consideration is what was going on in that woman’s mind."

McLean described the concession as a calculated move by a veteran trial attorney.

"By doing that, he is attempting to strip the prosecution of their shock value and force the jury to look purely at Lindsay Clancy’s mental capacity," she said.

Reddington argued that Clancy had no motive to kill children she had loved and nurtured. He also displayed graphic hospital photographs showing Clancy with injuries to her neck and wrists.

Lindsay Clancy's murder trial is expected to last six to eight weeks, and the witness list contains more than 200 names. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via Pool)

McLean said the defense was framing Clancy’s paralysis "not as a consequence of a crime, but as the tragic final symptom of a complete postpartum psychotic break."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse at Massachusetts General Hospital, has pleaded not guilty to three counts each of murder and strangulation. Her attorneys do not dispute that she killed the children but argue that she lacked criminal responsibility because of severe postpartum psychosis.

Judge William Sullivan told jurors that the Commonwealth must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Clancy was criminally responsible when the children were killed.

"It’s going to be black and white for some people, gray area for other people," McLean said. "It is going to be one of the hardest things that this jury, or any jury, will ever have to decide."

Sarah Rumpf-Whitten is a U.S. Writer at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to sarah.rumpf@fox.com and on X @s_rumpfwhitten

title: Hotelier stopped funding NSW Liberal ‘Reformers’ after deciding Morrison and Perrottet had ‘gone woke’, Icac hears
excerpt:
Michael O’Hara also tells corruption watchdog he was wrong to support young Liberals alleged to have solicited illegal donations, saying ‘I made a mistake’

Follow our Australia news live blog for lat...
body_text:
Michael O’Hara also tells corruption watchdog he was wrong to support young Liberals alleged to have solicited illegal donations, saying ‘I made a mistake’

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A witness who allegedly made prohibited donations to young New South Wales Liberal powerbrokers who planned to move the party to the right has told the corruption watchdog he is now “disgusted” by the scheme and “made a mistake” supporting the group.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Tuesday held its second day of Operation Rosny hearings into allegations of corruption against people associated with the NSW Liberal party.

In her opening statement on Monday, counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC said evidence would show how a group of young Liberal power brokers known as the “Reformers” allegedly solicited illegal donations to support branch stacking efforts to move the party to the conservative right.

In a separate allegation, she said that evidence would show members of the group anticipated receiving $2m from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif in exchange for outcomes sought by him.

On Tuesday, hotelier Michael O’Hara finished giving evidence to the inquiry . O’Hara, prohibited from making political donations because of his involvement in the liquor industry, is alleged to have paid $165,000 to the Reformers between 2018 and 2023.

“After what I heard yesterday and what I read in the newspapers … I am absolutely astounded by where it all ended up, which I had absolutely no knowledge of. I’m disgusted,” he said.

O’Hara admitted that he had made payments to registered lobbyist Beckington, founded by Reformers member Christian Ellis, and to a company controlled by Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of former Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet, to support branch-stacking efforts in Liberal branches in NSW, under the guise of financial advice or consulting services.

O’Hara was asked if he had discussed his donations to the Reformers during phone calls and text messages in September 2021 with now NSW shadow attorney general Damien Tudehope, his former business partner, following concerns O’Hara had about an anti-vaccination stance the group had taken.

“Well, the records show that I’ve spoken to him … I don’t recall the conversation,” he said. Asked if the contact would have included concerns about his support for the Reformers, O’Hara said: “It would appear so, yes.”

The inquiry heard O’Hara made his final payment in 2023 to the Reformers after coming to believe that the NSW Liberals under Dominic Perrottet had become “woke”.

“I may as well support the Greens or Teals, as Dominic was rolled on so many issues instead of prosecuting the principles I believed he stood for,” he allegedly wrote in an email to Jean-Claude Perrottet, who has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Explaining another message to Jean-Claude Perrottet, O’Hara told Icac his criticism of Perrottet was that “either he agrees with the woke crap that [former treasurer] Matt Kean was going on with, or else he was too weak to bring him into line. Either way, he was losing – he was showing he lost his spine”.

O’Hara told the inquiry that Scott “Morrison, the federal leader, had also gone woke, from Australia first, to exporting jobs overseas. He became weak, too”.

O’Hara said since hearing Dwyer’s opening statement, he now thought the Reformers’ scheme was “disgusting”. “I made a mistake in supporting them because they obviously went off the track,” he said.

Under cross-examination from his lawyer, Paul McGirr, O’Hara said it was not his understanding at the time that his payments to the Reformers were political donations.

On Tuesday, the current NSW Liberal leader, Kellie Sloane, who was not an MP at the time of the allegations Icac is investigating, told 2GB the first day of hearings had been “intensely uncomfortable listening”.

She said she stood by comments that Tudehope was a “man of integrity”. Tudehope, who is not accused of any wrongdoing, has stood aside from his roles as leader of the Liberals in the upper house and shadow attorney general after being called as a witness during the inquiry.

Sloane called for “procedurual fairness” to be observed after another member of her front bench, shadow finance minister Eleni Petinos, was named by Dwyer in her opening statement.

On Monday, the inquiry heard a legally intercepted phone call featuring Nassif in October 2021, in which he allegedly claimed he had paid for the removal of the building commissioner, David Chandler, and said that “the fair trading minister is gonna to be one of my girls”.

The inquiry heard that two months after the call, then Liberal premier Dominic Perrottet appointed Petinos as state minister of fair trading in a cabinet reshuffle. In July 2022, Chandler handed in his resignation following an investigation into his conduct that had been requested by Petinos. He was later cleared of any wrongdoing.

Dominic Perrottet and Petinos, who is currently on maternity leave, are not accused of any wrongdoing. Nassif, who fled Australia for Lebanon in 2022, has previously denied any wrongdoing and has declined a request to appear before the inquiry.

title: Ukraine’s Zelenskyy set to meet Trump as Iran and Ukraine wars converge
excerpt: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to meet United States President Donald Trump in the White House on Tuesday, a meeting that could coincide with the introduction of tough new sanctio...
body_text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is expected to meet United States President Donald Trump in the White House on Tuesday, a meeting that could coincide with the introduction of tough new sanctions on Russia.

Zelenskyy, who will attend the funeral of US Senator Lindsey Graham, ⁠is also scheduled to meet ‌with the Senate on ⁠Tuesday ⁠evening, the Reuters news agency reported, citing two Senate aides.

The vote on Russia sanctions, legislation that has been pending for months and was championed by Graham, could happen that same day.

If enacted, the Russian sanctions bill would ratchet up pressure on Moscow by imposing 100 percent tariffs on goods from the five largest importers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India.

In a last-minute intervention, Trump sought to add sanctions on Iran to the same bill.  Zelenskyy told Trump ally Laura Loomer last week that he thinks the move is a “great idea”.

The two wars, taking place roughly 2,500km (1,550 miles) apart, have converged in recent days.

On Saturday, Ukraine attacked an Iranian tanker in the Caspian Sea that Ukraine’s ambassador to Israel, Yevgen Korniychuk, said was carrying drones and military components from Iran to Russia. Iran has promised to retaliate.

By attacking Iranian ships, Kyiv is not only doing itself a favour but also attacking Washington’s “enemy number one”, which will please the US, former US ambassador to Kazakhstan and Georgia, William Courtney, told Al Jazeera.

But while Zelenskyy supports Iranian sanctions as part of the Russian sanctions bill, Ukraine is unlikely to want to be too closely associated with the “unpopular” US war on Iran, he added.

The US no longer provides direct financial aid to Ukraine for its war against the Russian invasion, but it still provides crucial intelligence for long-range strikes and sells weapons to Europe that are then passed on to Ukraine.

While their relationship seemed tense during a heated exchange in the White House in February 2025, relations between Zelenskyy and Trump have improved significantly in recent months.

The two leaders agreed earlier this month to allow Ukraine to jointly produce Patriot air defence interceptors, a crucial component for the country’s defence against Russian aerial attacks.

Ukraine and the US are also moving closer to a deal on joint drone production, a move that could help the US catch up with Ukraine in this crucial military technology.

Ukraine is on track to produce 6 to 7 million short-range attack drones this year, while the Pentagon’s $1.1bn production programme will have ordered just under 200,000 drones cumulatively by February 2027.

Heavy fighting continues on Ukraine’s front lines, and long-range strikes are taking place almost every day.

On Monday, Russian strikes on eastern Ukraine killed seven people and ⁠injured more than 20, officials said.

In Russia’s Belgorod region, a Ukrainian drone struck ‌a ‌commercial building, killing one person and injuring two.

Fighting is heaviest in Ukraine’s Konstantinyvka and Pokrovsk directions, both of which are in the Donetsk region.

title: US warns hundreds of Boeing jets may require seat safety inspections
excerpt:
The US aviation authority has warned that seats on hundreds of Boeing 737 MAX planes could have been installed incorrectly and may require inspection.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said o...
body_text:
The US aviation authority has warned that seats on hundreds of Boeing 737 MAX planes could have been installed incorrectly and may require inspection.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said on Monday that the issue relates to 453 jets registered in the US and proposed requiring airlines to inspect the seats.

If not installed correctly, the seats could come loose during an emergency landing and “injure passengers and crew members”, the FAA said, adding that they could also “block the aisle and slow an evacuation”.

The proposed order would apply only to US-registered planes because the FAA does not regulate foreign airlines.

Regulators in other countries, however, often follow FAA orders when the issue affects aircraft operating in their markets.

A Boeing spokesperson told the Reuters news agency that the company had issued guidance to operators ‌on the matter in December 2025.

“We support the FAA making that guidance mandatory,” the spokesperson said in an email.

The warning adds to years of scrutiny of Boeing’s safety record.

A cabin panel blew off an Alaska Airlines 737 MAX 9 in January 2024, forcing an emergency landing and prompting the FAA to ground 171 jets.

Investigators later found that the panel was missing four key bolts.

The scrutiny intensified after a spate of other accidents around the world, as well as the death of Boeing whistleblower John Barnett in March 2024 while he was providing evidence for a safety lawsuit against the firm.

In June 2025, the US National Transportation Safety Board said Boeing had failed to provide adequate training, guidance and oversight to prevent the Alaska Airlines incident.

There are nearly 2,300 737 MAX jets operating around the world, including 823 in the US, according to aviation advisory and intelligence firm IBA.

title: Well-connected Melbourne man found guilty of raping former staffer
excerpt:
Jury finds that the man, who cannot be named, assaulted the woman at his home in March 2023

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news...
body_text:
Jury finds that the man, who cannot be named, assaulted the woman at his home in March 2023

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A well-connected Melbourne man has been found guilty of raping a former employee.

The man, who cannot be named, faced two counts of rape and one count of sexual assault in the county court of Victoria, and pleaded not guilty.

After a three-week trial the jury found him guilty of all charges on Tuesday, after deliberating since late on Friday morning.

The man immediately had his bail revoked, and was taken into custody, but will be sentenced at a later date.

The assault occurred in March 2023, after the woman said she spent an evening drinking and taking cocaine with the man, while listening to music and watching the football at his friend’s home.

Both the prosecution and the defence argued that the most important witness was the alleged victim – the man’s former personal assistant – who gave evidence over more than four days before a closed court. The man did not give evidence during the trial.

The judge, Frank Gucciardo, thanked the jury after the verdict for their commitment during the trial.

“Those of us who have worked with juries for a very long time genuinely believe it’s the best system for determining matters like these,” he said.

“From time to time you hear people say that these cases should be judged by experts or lawyers or others, but those of us who have worked with juries know this is the best system we have.”

The prosecutor, Matthew Fisher, said given the man was likely to face a significant custodial sentence he should be taken into custody.

In his closing address to the jury, Fisher said some of the inconsistencies in the woman’s evidence had proved her credibility, as it showed she had not made it up.

But Dermot Dann KC, representing the man, described that as a “desperate submission”. He said the prosecution had asked the jury to swallow a “horrible mixture of lies, fabrications, inconsistencies [and] evidence that has been shown to be demonstrably untrue”.

Gucciardo told the jury in his final remarks before they retired to consider their verdict that the case was not about consent as the defence case was that no sexual contact had occurred.

At the start of the trial, Fisher said the offences had taken place when the woman was at the man’s house, where he tried to kiss her and sexually assaulted her.

She pushed his hands away and told him “I don’t want this”, Fisher told the court, to which the man responded with comments like “You’re so sexy”, “I can’t sleep, help me” and “I need this”.

The woman then felt the man rape her twice, Fisher said.

“She turned around to face him, and at that point she punched him with her fist to his face, to his nose,” Fisher told the court.

“He grabbed his face and said words to the effect of ‘you’ve broken my nose’.

“She got out of bed and said to him: ‘You’re a fucking rapist.’”

The woman went to another room and started taking notes of what happened on her phone, before texting her mother. Her mother called the police despite her daughter’s reluctance to involve them, the court heard.

The police arrived at the property about 3am on 24 March 2023.

Police then spoke to the woman, with the exchange recorded on a body-worn camera. The footage of that 35-minute conversation was shown to the jury.

The trial heard that woman worked as the man’s personal assistant for several months during the previous year, and the pair had resumed contact to discuss other employment opportunities when he invited her to his property.

Dann told the court that none of the offences had occurred. He said the woman had claimed she continued to stay in the house after the alleged offences.

He also said she was reluctant to contact authorities because of a prior allegation involving police but that allegation had been found to be false.

Dann also questioned why she had raised the issue of “recompense” with her mother while she was still at the man’s house.

The court also heard evidence from two of the man’s friends, who saw him and the woman in the hours before the offences, along with another former personal assistant and a friend of the alleged victim.

Two men – a former colleague and a barrister who met the accused when they both served on the board of a prominent Melbourne organisation – also gave character evidence in the trial.

title: Jacinta Allan resigns as Victorian premier in face of leadership challenge by Ben Carroll
excerpt:
Premier steps down from top job before expected spill, saying her deputy has her ‘unqualified support’

Live updates: Jacinta Allan quits as premier of Victoria

Get our breaking news email, free app ...
body_text:
Premier steps down from top job before expected spill, saying her deputy has her ‘unqualified support’

Live updates: Jacinta Allan quits as premier of Victoria

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Ben Carroll will become the next premier of Victoria, after Jacinta Allan resigned and a surprise rival for the Labor leadership emerged after a tumultuous 48 hours for Labor just four months out from the state election.

Speaking outside a party room meeting on Tuesday, Labor MP Juliana Addison announced that Carroll had been “unanimously endorsed by the state parliamentary Labor party as our next premier of Victoria”.

The transport infrastructure minister, Gabrielle Williams, secured the party’s deputy leadership.

Allan on Monday had vowed to contest a leadership ballot after a group of MPs told her she no longer had the support of caucus and urged her to stand down. Carroll, the deputy premier, also confirmed he would nominate for the Labor leadership.

But on Tuesday morning, Allan said on Tuesday morning that Carroll would have her “unqualified support”.

It was expected that Carroll would run unopposed for the leadership during Tuesday’s caucus meeting, avoiding a weeks’ long process to allow the broader party membership to vote.

But in a surprise move, Labor sources said frontbencher Sonya Kilkenny initially announced she would contest the leadership during the meeting, in which MPs could be heard shouting.

A contested leadership would have meant weeks of instability in the run-up to the election, as the party’s balloting process can take up to six weeks.

Speaking before the party room meeting on Tuesday, Allan said she had decided to step aside – despite believing she would have won a leadership ballot – because it was “the right thing” to do for Labor and Victorians.

“After speaking with my colleagues overnight, I have made the difficult decision to step aside as leader of the Victorian state parliamentary Labor party, and as premier of Victoria,” she said.

“I was prepared to put my record and my plan to a ballot of members as our rules allow. I believe I would have won. But doing this so this close to an election takes up valuable resources, including the most precious one – time.”

Allan said she would instead chair Tuesday’s caucus meeting to elect a new leader.

Speculation about a leadership spill had been swirling for months, and momentum had been building before parliament rose for the winter break in June. Poor polling and Allan’s weak personal approval ratings contributed to the push, along with rising support for One Nation.

Allan’s leadership has also been dogged by allegations of wrongdoing on the Big Build, as she was the minister responsible for transport infrastructure at the time. While she has apologised for criminal conduct that has been uncovered, she has also rejected calls for a royal commission. This is understood to have put her at odds with a number of MPs who believe the issue cannot be contained without one.

Carroll is understood to be in favour of a royal commission. He has also indicated that he believes he’d be better able to resolve the pay dispute between the government and public school teachers, improve the party’s economic credentials and do more to support businesses.

He had long been touted as a potential challenger for the leadership but consistently ruled out doing so. In June he looked Allan in the eye and declared he would not challenge her.

Under Labor’s rules, a contested leadership triggers an election process in which both the parliamentary caucus and rank-and-file Labor members vote, and can take a full six weeks to complete.

Arriving at parliament on Tuesday morning, Carroll made only a brief statement to reporters, saying his focus was on talking to his colleagues.

Before she announced her resignation, Steve Dimopoulos, a minister and key supporter of Allan, said: “I think the party has been good at sorting things out, this is what today will be.”

The former health minister Mary-Anne Thomas, who this year announced she would resign at the November election, said Allan had “served this state with real leadership. She’s always had the people of Victoria at the heart of everything that she does.”

The environment minister, Enver Erdogan, had told reporters on Tuesday morning there was a “case for change”. “I think we know some of these issues have been aired publicly but I think we need stronger action on crime and corruption in the state.”

Asked whether there needed to be a royal commission into allegations of corruption on Big Build construction sites, he replied: “Yes.”

title: Meta disregarded its own research on teen harm, Tennessee lawyers tell jury
excerpt:
In opening statements, state argued Meta’s own research showed it harmed teens while firm’s attorneys pointed to transparency

The long-awaited trial between the social media company Meta and the stat...
body_text:
In opening statements, state argued Meta’s own research showed it harmed teens while firm’s attorneys pointed to transparency

The long-awaited trial between the social media company Meta and the state of Tennessee began proceedings on Monday. Attorneys for Tennessee told a jury in Nashville that Meta, which owns Instagram and Facebook, disregarded internal research about its platform’s impact on teenagers, while the company sought ⁠to maximize profit from those young users.

During ⁠opening statements in a seven-week ​trial in state court, the state’s lawyers said Meta researchers repeatedly flagged teenagers’ compulsive use of the platform – leading to eating disorders, depression and self-harm. But despite those warnings, Meta did not ⁠disable features such as autoplay, notifications and infinite scroll which, the lawyers said, were designed to keep teens on Instagram as long as possible and increase the number of ads they viewed.

An attorney for Meta countered the company has been transparent ⁠about the risks teens face on Instagram and the amount of dangerous content it finds. The company works hard to find problems and fix them, the attorney said.

Tennessee’s lawsuit is one of 42 cases brought against Meta by individual states across the US. It comes after the company suffered a damaging loss in New Mexico in March, where a jury found the company liable for harming children and ordered it to pay $375m in civil penalties. It also comes as thousands of other lawsuits have been filed against Meta and other social media companies by families, school districts and state attorneys general.

The lawsuit in Tennessee, filed by attorney general Jonathan Skrmetti’s office, seeks financial penalties ‌and a court order directing Instagram to modify aspects of the platform that the state says are harmful to teens’ mental health.

If the jury finds ‌Meta liable, the trial will enter a second phase where the judge will decide damages.

During the opening statements, Tom Cartmell, a lawyer for the state, said Instagram triggers dopamine hits that promote addiction and that has a particularly strong impact on the brains of kids.

Cartmell also showed the jury an internal document from 2017 in which Meta product managers wrote that features such as notifications and infinite scroll “are inherently at odds with well-being” and said that the company needed to warn ​the public.

“This warning never came,” Cartmell said.

Kevin Huff, a lawyer for Meta, said documents such as those Cartmell cited are proof that the company is searching for problems on its platforms, so it can improve them. The company has developed tools to help limit problematic use of Instagram, Huff said, and seeks to empower teachers and parents to help keep teens safe.

“We think the evidence will show that Meta is doing its part and empowering others to ​do their part, because protecting teens online is a ​shared responsibility,” Huff said. “It takes a village.”

The next lawsuit over social media addiction and harm to children is slated to go to trial next month in Oakland, California. It will be the first federal trial against the social media companies, including Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap, and was brought by attorneys general from 29 states.

title: Asia ‘scraping the bottom of the barrel’ as Red Sea oil blockade worsens energy crisis
excerpt:
The Houthi threat to Saudi oil exports comes as Japan, South Korea and the Philippines are still reeling from the closure of the strait of Hormuz

Governments in Asia are scrambling to avoid their sec...
body_text:
The Houthi threat to Saudi oil exports comes as Japan, South Korea and the Philippines are still reeling from the closure of the strait of Hormuz

Governments in Asia are scrambling to avoid their second major energy crisis in six months, as another maritime chokepoint in the Middle East faces a violent blockade, leaving only the Suez canal completely open for the free movement of gulf oil.

Countries like Japan, the Philippines, Thailand and South Korea – which rely on Middle East oil for up to 90% of their imports – are working to secure supplies after Yemen’s Houthis launched a blockade of Saudi Arabian shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandab strait, which forms the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

Many countries in Asia are still reeling from Iran’s effective closure of the strait of Hormuz in March, which forced governments across the region to compete for increasingly dwindling supplies of Middle Eastern crude oil.

“They’re scraping at the bottom of the barrel in terms of global reserve capacity … there’s very little inventory now,” says Ahmed Helal, from the Asia Group thinktank.

Japan – along with neighbouring countries – is already spending billions on fuel subsidies to keep the cost of petroleum down, hitting government budgets hard. ⁠After the announcement from the Houthis, some like South Korea were quick to extend those fuel ​tax cuts.

Meanwhile, the spike in the cost of imports has led to a rise in inflation, piling pressure on the governments of regional giants such as Japan and Indonesia.

Now, the threat to Red Sea shipping is set to increase the pressure. In March, Saudi Arabia responded to the closure of the strait of Hormuz by rerouting oil exports from the gulf on the country’s east coast, to the west coast port of Yanbu in the Red Sea which now handles more than 70% of Riyadh’s crude oil exports.

That proved to be a lifeline for many Asian nations, like China – which is the largest buyer of Saudi oil – and India, Japan and South Korea, which follow close behind.

Some Japanese and South Korean refiners are reportedly seeking to circumvent the Houthi threat by rerouting cargos north through the Suez canal, to the Mediterranean and around Africa. But this lengthy detour comes with huge costs.

A VLCC, the largest size of oil tanker, is too big to pass through the Suez canal fully loaded, meaning cargos would need to unload up to half of their oil in the Red Sea, have it transported through Egypt’s Sumed pipeline to the Mediterranean coast, where they would then pick it up after transiting through the canal, adding costs and logistical complications to the journey.

Rerouting the oil via the Mediterranean and around the Cape of Good Hope would also more than double the voyage time for most Asian importers, further adding to freight and fuel costs.

For now, it’s a cost many may be willing to incur. The Houthis targeted at least two Saudi oil tankers exiting the Red Sea last week and launched attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure this week. The number of vessels transiting through Bab ⁠al-Mandab has fallen to the lowest level in months, with international shipping apparently paralysed by the Houthi threat.

“Changing behaviour by tankers tells us that they are ⁠taking the ​threats seriously,” says Matt Smith, a commodity research director at Kpler, a market tracker.

Insurers have responded in kind, with war risk premiums paid by tankers reportedly doubling in the last week, potentially adding hundreds of thousands of dollars to the cost of a voyage.

Those costs will inevitably be passed on to consumers in Asia, who are already reeling from the energy shock imposed by the US-Iran war.

“Businesses are going to have to close. You might have attempts to reduce consumption at peak hours. And you might have, in some extreme cases, higher risk of default,” says Helal.

After transits through the strait of Hormuz slowed to a halt in March, many countries in Asia rushed to mitigate the effects of the disruption. Coal-fired power plants blazed back into use, a four-day working week was imposed in Sri Lanka, while staff in Vietnam were urged to work from home. But now, resources and patience are running low.

The Houthi threat has inspired the Philippines, India and South Korea to all bolster their strategic reserves of oil and gas. Meanwhile across the region, the crisis has added a renewed urgency to the renewables transition.

But with no short-term solutions, Asian importers are reportedly looking farther afield for supplies, with Russia once again likely to benefit from chaos in the Middle East.

Earlier this year Japan and South Korea reportedly bought Russian oil for the first time since Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in ‌2022. In the past week, Reuters reported that Chinese refiner ramped up purchases ⁠of sanctioned Russian crude oil to counter the latest disruptions.

The disruption and chaos points to a truth that experts say governments in Asia have ignored for too long: their energy systems remain far too vulnerable.

Helal predicts this crisis will force many governments to reckon with their supply chains and their capacity to store strategic reserves.

But for now, they simply have to secure supplies, he says, because “there’s very little in the tank for them to draw on.”

body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A California family claims it was targeted in a racially motivated attack at a luxury Maui resort after a group allegedly hurled chairs and beat relatives ranging from teenagers to senior citizens during a chaotic poolside brawl.

Maui police confirmed to Fox News Digital that officers responded to the Kaanapali Alii resort in Lahaina on July 17 around 10 p.m. for a disorderly incident involving approximately 30 people. Police said when officers arrived they found 10 to 15 people still gathered near the pool, several with visible injuries.

Police confirmed the preliminary investigation identified seven California victims between the ages of 17 and 62 who reported that a large group of juveniles assaulted multiple members of their party before fleeing.

According to Maui police, one victim told investigators he and his family were near the pool when an unknown male ran toward them asking for help. Moments later, several juvenile males allegedly chased the individual into the area before turning their attention to others nearby.

CITIES BRACE FOR HOLIDAY WEEKEND TEEN TAKEOVERS PUTTING BYSTANDERS AT DEADLY RISK, FORMER PROSECUTOR WARNS

An aerial view of the Kaanapali Alii resort in Lahaina, Hawaii. (Kaanapali Alii Facebook)

"The group allegedly began throwing chairs and physically assaulting numerous people in the area, indiscriminately attacking individuals of all ages, including elderly family members who were struck during the incident," Maui police told Fox News Digital.

Family members told Hawaii News Now the alleged attackers repeatedly threatened to "beat up the haole boys" before the violence erupted.

Merriam-Webster defines "haole" as a Hawaiian term used to describe a foreigner or person of non-Hawaiian descent.

CRAZY BRAWL OVER A PARKING SPOT IN NEW YORK INCLUDES A VICIOUS SKATEBOARD TO THE HEAD

Low-angle view of the waters off Kaanapali Beach in Maui, Hawaii. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)

The family told the outlet it wants the assault investigated as a hate crime. Maui police have not classified the incident as a hate crime.

One of the most seriously injured victims was a relative who was struck in the head with a chair while trying to protect family members, suffering a severe head wound that required 13 staples, according to the family.

Police told Fox News Digital that the investigation led to the arrest of a 20-year-old Makawao man on suspicion of second-degree assault. He was later released as the investigation continues. The case is currently classified as an assault/riot, and detectives have interviewed those involved while continuing to gather evidence.

SOCIALIST-LED CALIFORNIA CITY'S CLASH OVER ISRAEL AND ANTISEMITISM OFFERS GLIMPSE INTO THE LEFT'S FUTURE

A Maui Police Department vehicle in Lahaina, Hawaii. (Maui Police Department Facebook)

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Kaanapali Alii said the safety and well-being of its guests, residents and team members "remains our highest priority" and that resort security responded immediately after the violence broke out.

"Upon learning of the altercation, our security team responded promptly, contacted the Maui Police Department and emergency medical services, and remained on scene to assist until first responders arrived," the resort said. "We have provided surveillance footage and are cooperating fully with law enforcement as their investigation continues."

The resort said it is also conducting its own internal review of the incident.

Addressing the family’s allegation that they were targeted because of their race, the resort said it takes claims of racial bias seriously but cautioned against drawing conclusions before detectives complete their investigation.

"We take allegations of this nature seriously," the statement said. "At this time, allegations regarding motive or the circumstances surrounding the incident have not been substantiated, and it would be inappropriate to speculate or draw conclusions while the investigation remains ongoing."

The resort also acknowledged that staff received reports of threats, harassment and disruptive behavior involving individuals connected to the incident before the violence erupted, but declined to discuss those complaints further because of the active criminal investigation.

Visitors walk along the Kaanapali Beachwalk amid palm trees and landscaped grounds overlooking Kaanapali North Beach at the Outrigger Honua Kai Resort and Spa, Lahaina, Maui, Hawaii, July 11, 2026. (Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images)

"Because this remains an active criminal investigation, we cannot comment on specific security actions, witness accounts or other details that could compromise the investigative process," the resort said.

The property said it remains committed to supporting investigators and those affected by the violence.

"Our focus remains on the well-being of our guests, residents and team members, and on assisting law enforcement in every way possible," the statement said.

Anyone with information or video related to the incident is asked to contact the Maui Police Department’s Criminal Investigation Division at (808) 244-6425.

title: Betye Saar, pioneering figure of Black arts movement, dies at 99
excerpt:
Leading assemblage artist was known for reclaiming Jim Crow-era memorabilia as images of Black liberation

Artist Betye Saar, the pioneering figure of the Black arts movement, died on Sunday morning i...
body_text:
Leading assemblage artist was known for reclaiming Jim Crow-era memorabilia as images of Black liberation

Artist Betye Saar, the pioneering figure of the Black arts movement, died on Sunday morning in her home town of Los Angeles. She was 99.

Saar, a famous practitioner of assemblage, an artistic style that builds sculpture from everyday objects, was best known for reclaiming Jim Crow era memorabilia such as dolls and washboards and recasting them as images of Black liberation. Saar also worked in genres including printmaking and film, exploring themes from family to spirituality.

“Her symbolically rich body of work has evolved over time to demonstrate the environmental, cultural, political, racial, technological, economic, and historical context in which it exists,” according to Roberts Projects, the Los Angeles gallery that represents her.

Saar began her career in design and shifted to art at the age of 35. She continued to make art into her 90s. Saar grew up in Pasadena and was part of a community of Black artists in nearby Altadena; she often cited Simon Rodia’s Watts Towers as an early source of inspiration.

Throughout her career, Saar combed flea markets and yard sales for discarded objects showing how consumer culture depicted Black Americans.

“My work has to do with recycling,” she told a documentary crew in the 1970s, according to the Los Angeles Times. “Each item I collect has a certain energy from its previous function that carries over into its new use.”

She is perhaps best known for her 1972 revolutionary reimagination of Aunt Jemima, the image once used to market a pancake mix and syrup brand founded at the tail-end of the 19th century. Aunt Jemima was based on “mammy” images that depicted enslaved Black women as contented domestic servants. Saar’s Liberation of Aunt Jemima holds a rifle in her left hand, and a grenade wedged between her right arm and chest.

Quaker Oats retired the Aunt Jemima image in 2021.

Saar work also used natural materials gathered from travels around the world exploring the African diaspora and spirituality.

“Wherever I go, I say, ‘What’s the alternative religion?’ because every country has it,” she said in a 2021 interview with the Guardian. “There are lots of other people that believe in magic and they have their own religion, and I was just really interested in what they did and what their ceremonies were, but mostly what the visual images would be.”

Saar taught and mentored a generation of Black artists, including the painter Kerry James Marshall. Saar has long been considered a leading figure of the west coast arts landscape.

In spring 2026, Saar was inducted to the American Academy of Arts and Letters.

title: Fauci's diary shows he fed questions to journalists, built friendships with media figures
excerpt:
The ‘Outnumbered’ panel discusses Dr. Anthony Fauci’s newly released diary entries that reveal his thoughts on fame and lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Dr. Anthony Fauci opened up about his r...
body_text:
The ‘Outnumbered’ panel discusses Dr. Anthony Fauci’s newly released diary entries that reveal his thoughts on fame and lockdowns during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Dr. Anthony Fauci opened up about his relationships with various media personalities in a series of controversial diary entries that put a spotlight on the former White House COVID advisor's cozy relationship with the press.

Fauci’s diary entries were released on Saturday by Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., detailing the doctor’s role during the COVID-19 crisis through conversations with President Donald Trump, governors, world leaders, media appearances and his personal observations as the pandemic unfolded in 2020. The stunning diary entries reveal that Fauci made fast friends with members of the liberal media who were tasked with covering the pandemic.

Fauci’s closest media ally appeared to have been CNN anchor Jake Tapper, who was mentioned 41 times in the eyebrow-raising diary.

ABC, NBC, CBS, CNN AND MS NOW IGNORE FAUCI DIARY ENTRIES THAT REVEAL FIXATION ON FAME DURING COVID

Dr. Anthony Fauci opened up about his relationships with various media personalities in a series of controversial diary entries.

According to the diary, Tapper texted Fauci to mock rival cable news hosts and other doctors. On one occasion, Tapper called to check on Fauci after an appearance on his show irked Trump supporters.

"Jake wanted to make sure the interview did not cause me any problems," Fauci wrote on April 13, 2020.

In July 2020, Fauci gushed that he was forming a friendship with Tapper.

"Had dinner over Jake Tapper and Jen Tapper’s home in DC. Terrific couple. Friendship building," Fauci wrote, according to the diary.

Later that month, Fauci wrote that he "gave Jake some questions to ask" pediatrician Brett Giroir during an interview on CNN’s "State of the Union." But Tapper would later express frustration, waking Fauci up in the process.

"Tapper woke me up at 11:23 AM (I went to bed early) furius [sic] at POTUS for tweeting about the fact that Jake severly [sic] questioned Brett Giroir on SOTU CNN show today. Jake was really pissed at the craziness of it all," Fauci wrote.

The late-night tirade couldn’t have bothered Fauci too much, as he invited Tapper to dinner at his home months later.

"Had dinner at my home with Jake and Jennifer Tapper. Relaxed, good time. Jake clearly believes that Trump is totally nuts," Fauci wrote on Oct. 23, 2020.

FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

CNN anchor Jake Tapper was mentioned 41 times by Fauci in his diary entries. (Bryan Bedder/Variety via Getty Images)

CNN’s Dana Bash sent Fauci a text message in April 2021 after a contentious House Select Subcommittee hearing over COVID-19, according to the diary. The CNN star complimented Fauci and informed the doctor that her CNN colleague also picked a side.

"Dana Bash sent me a text: ‘I just watched the whole Jordan thing. Again, you’re a better man than I …. As our friend Wolf Blitzer said to me yesterday — no one would have blamed you if you said simply ‘Mr. Jordan, go f--- yourself,’" Fauci wrote.

Tapper and Bash went on to moderate the CNN Republican Presidential Primary Debate between then-President Biden and President Trump in 2024.

Meanwhile, Andrea Mitchell celebrated July 4, 2020, by offering a mea culpa to Fauci, who believed the White House was limiting his TV exposure.

"Andrea Mitchell called my cell very apologetic about not being able to have me on the show since they already booked a couple of governors who were giving exclusives to NBC. I mentioned to her my concern about them keeping me off the air. She was shocked and thought that when I did not come on after requests that it was because I did not want to go on a show," Fauci wrote.

INSIDE FAUCI'S PRIVATE DIARY: WHAT HE WROTE ABOUT TRUMP, TV PERSONALITIES AND CELEBRITIES

Fauci wrote in his diary that CNN anchor Dana Bash sent him a text expressing support for him following a contentious exchange he had on Capitol Hill with Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio. (Maya Dehlin Spach/FilmMagic)

Fauci also had a texting relationship with then-NBC News host Chuck Todd.

"I had a really nice conversation with Chuck Todd this morning. He had texted me to ask what I thought of the interview yesterday. I told him that I thought it was absolutely terrific, but I wanted some advice from him. I asked him whether he thought that I should pull back from publicly defending myself against the slanderous attacks since that might call more attention to them," Fauci wrote.

Fauci also revealed that ABC’s George Stephanopoulos texted him following an interview on "Good Morning America" in July 2020. Apparently, Stephanopoulos was impressed that Fauci dismissed a mean tweet from Trump.

"Thank you, Tony. So impressive," Stephanopoulos wrote, according to the diary.

Fauci boasted early in the diary that he prepped CBS News chief medical correspondent Dr. Jonathan LaPook for a TV appearance.

"Also, Jon LaPook was interviewed on CBS Morning News and mentioned me several times since he e-mailed (sic) me over the weekend to prep him for his interview on Universal Flu vaccine and HIV vaccines," Fauci wrote.

Representatives for NBC News, ABC News and CBS News did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment. A spokesperson for CNN declined to comment.

Brian Flood is a media editor/reporter for FOX News Digital. Story tips can be sent to brian.flood@fox.com and on Twitter: @briansflood.
