title: New Jersey governor signs law banning surveillance pricing to protect shoppers
excerpt:
New law prohibits retailers from using personal data to charge different prices for identical products

New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill recently signed a new law prohibiting businesses from using s...
body_text:
New law prohibits retailers from using personal data to charge different prices for identical products

New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill recently signed a new law prohibiting businesses from using shoppers’ personal information to charge different prices for identical products, making her state the third in the US to ban the practice.

The Fair Price Protection Act passed by New Jersey’s legislature seeks to protect consumers from surveillance pricing, in which retailers can use data including online activity, location and purchasing history to arbitrarily change prices for individual shoppers.

“New Jersey families are already feeling the pressure of higher costs,” Sherrill said in a statement after signing the law. “The last thing they need is companies secretly using their personal data to charge them more than someone else for the exact same product.

“If businesses want to compete, they should do so by offering better prices, not by finding new ways to squeeze shoppers. This law puts New Jersey shoppers first by protecting their privacy and ensuring fairness in pricing.”

New Jersey’s Fair Price Protection Act follows similar measures in Maryland and Connecticut, which have both banned surveillance pricing. Meanwhile, a similar bill awaiting a signature from Governor Kathy Hochul in New York would ban personalized price manipulation.

According to Sherrill’s office, the law prohibits businesses from using shoppers’ personal data to set individualized prices on groceries and other essential items. It does not, however, apply to loyalty programs or other discounts.

Sherrill’s office added that the law also pauses the rollout of new electronic shelf labels for one year while the New Jersey Innovation Authority studies their impact. Stores could continue using, repairing and replacing existing electronic shelf labels.

Hailing the pause on electronic shelf labels, Ademola Oyefeso, vice-president of the labor union United Food and Commercial Workers International, said: “The law’s moratorium on the use of electronic shelf labels is an important step to ensure this technology does not harm New Jersey shoppers or workers.”

She added: “We hope this law will serve as a catalyst for states across the country to shield shoppers from … predatory pricing” set by artificial intelligence “and protect good, union grocery jobs”.

title: Lando Norris wins Hungarian Grand Prix for first F1 triumph in 2026
excerpt:
Lando Norris has ended an eight-month wait for a Formula One victory with strong pace and a dose of good fortune to win the Hungarian Grand Prix on Sunday.

McLaren’s defending champion finished ahead...
body_text:
Lando Norris has ended an eight-month wait for a Formula One victory with strong pace and a dose of good fortune to win the Hungarian Grand Prix on Sunday.

McLaren’s defending champion finished ahead of Max Verstappen in Red Bull and teenage sensation Kimi Antonelli at the Hungaroring circuit in Budapest on Sunday.

Norris was on pole but lost the lead to his McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri when he ran wide at the second corner, before reclaiming the lead after Piastri was delayed by a collision with Carlos Sainz Jr during a lap.

This allowed Norris to come out of the pits ahead of his teammate and cruise to a win.

“The car was unbelievable today. Well done guys, incredible. We were flying,” Norris said. “Nice to finally be able to do it all for you. Feels like it’s been a while.”

Piastri then stopped with a broken gearbox, paving the way for Verstappen to take second, with Antonelli third.

Antonelli increased his standings lead, with title rival Lewis Hamilton finishing fifth after a penalty for speeding in the pits and George Russell seventh after a near-stall at the start.

Norris hadn’t won a full Grand Prix race since Sao Paulo in November, though he did win a sprint in Miami in May.

Hungary was the last race before the mid-season break. The next race is the Dutch Grand Prix on August 23.

title: 'Shark Tank' star Daymond John says 'you'll be screwed' if you do this when starting a business
excerpt:
The 57-year-old businessman told Fox News Digital you have to be passionate about whatever business you are starting and shouldn't do it just for the money.

"Shark Tank" star Daymond John is giving f...
body_text:
The 57-year-old businessman told Fox News Digital you have to be passionate about whatever business you are starting and shouldn't do it just for the money.

"Shark Tank" star Daymond John is giving fans some blunt advice on how to be successful in business.

When speaking to Fox News Digital at Fanatics Fest, the 57-year-old businessman shared that to have a successful business, you have to build it around "something that you love."

"If you're starting something that you love, you have to want to do it for free. I always say to kids, you know, you got to get paid for what you'd do for free, you'd be able to sell whatever you would buy. So, any business is a great business. Emptying garbage is a great business if you really love it. If you're doing it just for money though, you'll be screwed. Even Kevin O'Leary, you think he does it for money? No, he just likes complicated structures that manage his downside. But at the end of the day, he likes the chess game."

The reality TV star began working at a young age, developing his entrepreneurial spirit before founding FUBU ("For Us, By Us") in 1992 along with three of his childhood friends.

DIGITAL ENTREPRENEUR CREDITS THE WORLD CUP WITH TEACHING ABOUT SOCCER AND BOOSTING HER MONTHLY INCOME

Daymond John advised young entrepreneurs to build a business around something they love and would buy themselves. (Michael Yarish/WBTV via Getty Images)

Now a global fashion brand, the business began with John sewing wool hats and T-shirts himself in his mother's house in Queens, New York.

"First of all, I was frustrated by Timberland, and a couple of other people and brands that 'didn’t make clothes for African Americans,'" he told The Source Magazine. "That was why I initially created FUBU. It was my love of fashion as well and my love for music. And I felt that no longer did we have to have the 'make it and they will come theory' like other designers."

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

He continued: "I was a designer who actually respected the community I was selling to, and it was fun. It was an exciting time. Hip-hop was young and fresh, and I was just happy to wear the clothes that I was making as well as seeing artists and other people wear the clothes that I was making for them."

WATCH: ‘SHARK TANK’ STAR DAYMOND JOHN SHARES WHAT WILL GET YOU ‘SCREWED’ IN BUSINESS

After turning FUBU into a global fashion brand, John joined the original cast of "Shark Tank" in 2009, alongside Barbara Corcoran, O'Leary, Robert Herjavec and Kevin Harrington.

John was cast on "Shark Tank" in 2009. (Christopher Willard/Disney via Getty Images)

As a shark, John has invested in a number of businesses, helping entrepreneurs get them off the ground. Some of his most famous investments include Bombas and Bubba's-Q Boneless Ribs.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I always look for the person first — before the idea," he told Inc. about his investing philosophy. "I need to know that they are going to get the right information, and not go off and make mistakes without at least trying to educate themselves. I value an entrepreneur I can get behind and trust because I know they are attempting to move forward in life."

While at Fanatics Fest, John told Fox News Digital, "I'm just here being a fan myself." (Disney/Christopher Willard)

While at Fanatics Fest, a Comic-Con style celebration and immersive sports festival, John told Fox News Digital he was looking forward to experiencing everything the festival had to offer as a fan.

"I haven't gotten to see most of it, but for three years in, I mean, this is nuts, right? It's everything from WWE to UFC, to, of course, all the sports stuff, the signing, the trading, all of the celebrities and the sports people here. I'm just here being a fan myself," he said.

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

title: Australia news live: new Sydney Harbour pool slated to open in summer; AusAlert warning test to blare siren across phones nationally
excerpt:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Speculation has been mounting overnight that Victoria’s Labor premier Jacinta Allan will face a leadership challenge this week, just four m...
body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Speculation has been mounting overnight that Victoria’s Labor premier Jacinta Allan will face a leadership challenge this week, just four months from an election.

Factional conveners from Labor’s left and right met on Sunday night to discuss whether Allan still had the support of a majority of the caucus. It is understood the group agreed she did not.

But the pathway to a leadership challenge remains unclear as Allan’s most likely opponent – the deputy premier, Ben Carroll – has indicated to colleagues he would only run if the position was vacant.

A key figure at the centre of an anti-corruption inquiry involving the New South Wales Liberal party has moved to the UK and is not expected to give evidence during eight weeks of public hearings.

The Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) will start its Operation Rosny hearings on Monday. The first witness will be hotelier Michael O’Hara, followed later in the week by former Liberal staffer Dylan Whitelaw and consultant Robert Assaf.

O’Hara and Assaf are among 10 individuals Icac has said it is investigating. Whitelaw is not named in the Icac allegations.

Christian Ellis, a former registered lobbyist and Liberal powerbroker who once received a glowing endorsement from the federal opposition leader, Angus Taylor, is named in two Icac allegations but is not expected to appear.

A 2023 parliamentary inquiry preceded Icac’s current examination of “possible offences under the Electoral Funding Act”. Since that parliamentary inquiry, Ellis has moved to the UK, Guardian Australia can reveal.

Speculation has been mounting overnight that Victoria’s Labor premier Jacinta Allan will face a leadership challenge this week, just four months from an election.

Factional conveners from Labor’s left and right met on Sunday night to discuss whether Allan still had the support of a majority of the caucus. It is understood the group agreed she did not.

But the pathway to a leadership challenge remains unclear as Allan’s most likely opponent – the deputy premier, Ben Carroll – has indicated to colleagues he would only run if the position was vacant.

Morning folks, Stephanie Convery with you here to bring you all the live news today. Thanks so much to my colleagues for kicking us off this morning.

Cam McEvoy has dominated the 50m freestyle final in Glasgow, breaking the Commonwealth Games record, AAP reports.

McEvoy, who broke the world record in March, was the only finalist to crack 21 seconds as he led home an Australian medal sweep.

The 32-year-old dad clocked 20.97 seconds to beat Flynn Southam’s 21.44, while Jamie Jack took bronze in 21.47.

It is McEvoy’s first individual Commonwealth Games gold medal.

Two more bird flu cases confirmed in South Australia

Two local birds in South Australia suspected to have a deadly bird flu, greater crested terns found in Robe and Semaphore, have been confirmed positive for the H5N1 virus by CSIRO.

This takes the total of H5 confirmed or presumed positive detections to 20 nationally, Australia’s acting chief veterinary officer, Dr Sam Hamilton, said in a Sunday statement.

double quotation markAll of these have been individual wild seabirds found in coastal locations.

There remains no evidence of any mass mortality events and there are no detections in poultry or in our agricultural production system.

NSW planning minister calls for bill to allow commercial activity around new pool

The planning and public services minister, Paul Scully, said the Callan park upgrades represented a “new era”.

“The new tidal baths and return of 1.6 hectares, or the equivalent of 4,000 large picnic blankets of green open space, to the community will mean more people can enjoy this great parkland,” he said on Monday.

Scully argued Callan park would be further improved by the Parklands bill, which passed the state’s lower house in May and was now before the Legislative Council. Legislation currently prevents any commercial activity in Callan park.

“For the park to be able to host your new favourite café and reach its full potential, we need the … bill to pass parliament,” Scully said.

When opened, the Callan park baths will be the latest of Sydney’s new or re-animated public swimming spots. Marrinawi Cove at Barangaroo was dubbed Sydney’s first city beach in 50 years when it opened in 2023.

Bayview park on the Parramatta River reopened for swimming in 2022 after being closed for more than five decades. The river also boasts Chiswick baths and Cabarita beach, while “Pondi” – Penrith beach – was opened in Castlereagh in 2024.

Sydney’s latest harbour swimming pool, on the banks of Callan Park in Lilyfield, will open for swimmers this summer, the state government says, with construction now under way.

The new tidal baths on the Iron Cove foreshore, along the popular Bay Run and close to sports fields like Leichhardt Oval and King George Park, is expected to attract thousands to the southern banks of the Parramatta River.

Demolition work has also started on nine unsafe buildings in Callan park “which were neglected for so long that they have become not only an eyesore but a safety hazard”, the Minns government said on Monday.

“The removal of these long cordoned off buildings will unlock central parts of Callan Park, delivering the equivalent of two football fields of green space back to free community use,” the government said in a statement.

The baths will include a shark net, a fixed jetty, a pontoon, and an accessible pathway and ramp into the water.

Construction of the new tidal baths was expected to take six months, meaning it should open for summer 2026. The building demolition in Callan park was also expected to be completed by the end of this year.

Stephanie Convery will be with you soon to take you through today’s news as it unfolds.

At 2pm AEST today, most phones in the country will blare an emergency siren as part of the first nationwide test of the new AusAlert warning system. People who may have secret “safe phones”, kept hidden for personal safety reasons, have been advised to consider turning off their devices for up to 24 hours after the test and drivers have been warned not to touch their phones during the alert.

The Royal Commission on Anti-semitism and Social Cohesion continues in Sydney.

And Ed Husic is up on ABC Radio soon to talk about fallout from the national Labor conference.

title: Home cocktail maker says Gen Z isn't giving up alcohol — they're changing how they drink
excerpt:
Fox News' Madison Scarpino provides details on the apparent shift away from alcohol consumption in the U.S. as natural sleep aid supplements increase in popularity.

The alcohol industry has long reli...
body_text:
Fox News' Madison Scarpino provides details on the apparent shift away from alcohol consumption in the U.S. as natural sleep aid supplements increase in popularity.

The alcohol industry has long relied on young adults eventually becoming regular drinkers. Now, Gen Z is forcing the industry to shift as they embrace "sober-curious" lifestyles and search for quality beverages.

A 2025 Gallup poll found that the percentage of U.S. adults who said that they consume alcohol fell to 54%, the lowest rate in the 90 years it had been tracking. From 1997 to 2023, Gallup found that at least 60% of Americans reported drinking alcohol. The figure fell to 58% in 2024 and again to 54% in 2025.

The alcohol industry faces a new challenge. Rather than simply getting young adults to become lifelong customers, they now must convince them that their product is worth the price.

GEN Z STILL DRINKS, JUST EARLIER AS THE 'DAYCAP' TREND BEGINS UPENDING NIGHTLIFE

Bartesian CEO Ryan Close says consumers are seeking premium experiences, opening new opportunities for the at-home cocktail industry. (Courtesy of Bartesian)

Ryan Close, the CEO and founder of Bartesian, said he is seeing consumers choose quality over quantity. He said they are not looking to consume more or less alcohol, but rather they're searching for better and higher-quality beverage options.

"I'm not gonna argue with the data, you know, they probably are drinking less alcohol. I think they're drinking less, but with the expectation that 'I want better,'" he told Fox News Digital, regarding Gen Z's drinking habits.

Bartesian makes an automated at-home cocktail machine that allows users to create bar-style cocktails by inserting flavor capsules and adding their own spirits.

Close told Fox News Digital that before starting Bartesian, he noticed people were mostly drinking wine and beer at home, despite ordering cocktails while out at bars and restaurants. He said many found cocktails to be too difficult and that they did not want to gather all the necessary bitters and other ingredients. Despite having years of bartending experience, Close struggled to make a classic cocktail: the Old Fashioned, a flavor that is available in Bartesian pods.

Close said that his company was built around the idea that consumers wanted premium cocktails at home that are made with good ingredients.

"We only use real ingredients so we're not putting anything artificial, no artificial colors or flavors in the cocktails, so, you're just getting that true quality freshness," he said.

HIGH-ALCOHOL, READY-TO-DRINK COCKTAILS SPARK OVERCONSUMPTION CONCERNS FOR GEN Z DRINKERS

Bartesian CEO Ryan Close believes younger consumers are looking for premium experiences rather than drinking for the sake of drinking. (Mediaphotos via iStock/Getty Images)

Industry research suggests Close is not the only one noticing the shift toward a search for quality. In a Jan. 2 report outlining five consumer trends shaping the alcohol industry, NielsenIQ (NIQ) identified a similar pattern among drinkers. NIQ found that 67% of spirits drinkers and around half (52%) of average drinkers said they would be willing to pay more for higher quality drinks. Though NIQ's report looked at on-premises patterns, not at-home drinking.

Close believes the shift is going beyond what consumers drink and expanding to why they're drinking in the first place. He argued that Gen Z consumers are not looking to "drink for the sake of drinking," but are instead seeking to have a shared experience. Bartesian not only allows users to pick different flavors of cocktails, but also what kind of spirits and how much alcohol goes into the drinks, something Close said leans into this idea of wanting an experience.

"I just think the younger generation is more intentional and it's not about, 'Hey, I don't wanna drink at all,' it's, 'I wanna drink better, less often, and more quality,'" Close told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Bartesian machines allow users to pick the type of spirits that go into their cocktails and the strength of their drinks. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)

Many older Gen Z consumers turned 21 during the COVID-19 pandemic, as restaurants and bars across the country were closed or operating under tight restrictions. Close said he believes younger consumers are increasingly viewing the home as "an extension of restaurants and bars," creating a demand for premium at-home cocktail experiences.

Close said rising cocktail prices have only accelerated that shift, as consumers become more selective about how they spend their money. He recalled that during a recent trip to New York City, he found himself paying around $24 for a martini that was missing a key ingredient — blue cheese olives.

"I'm not looking to spend $75 on martinis when I know — especially without the blue cheese — when I can go home and make that exact same cocktail for $3 or $4," he said.

The trend, according to Close, is not about replacing bars and restaurants altogether, but rather meeting consumer demand who are more deliberate about what they drink, where they drink it and the value of experiences.

Rachel Wolf is a media and culture reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: US and Iran hit pause on strikes for second day
excerpt:
The United States and Iran have pressed pause on what had been an escalating conflict for a second day.

Reports on Sunday said neither the US nor Iran had launched strikes for a second day in a row. ...
body_text:
The United States and Iran have pressed pause on what had been an escalating conflict for a second day.

Reports on Sunday said neither the US nor Iran had launched strikes for a second day in a row. The sudden period of calm after two weeks of nightly attacks on Iran by the US and Iranian retaliation on US allies in the Gulf came amid hopes of a return to diplomacy.

US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told Fox News on Sunday that President Donald Trump was “giving [the potential for] talks … a little bit of room”.

While noting that the president has said the US was “locked and loaded,” Waltz said negotiators have been engaged at every level over the past few weeks, and in particular, over the past few days.

US broadcaster CBS, quoting two regional sources, reported that the US decision to pause the bombing was made due to the arrival in Tehran of a delegation from Oman.

The New York Times reported that Trump paused plans to escalate attacks due to concerns about draining the Pentagon’s diminishing stockpile of missile interceptors and other air defence munitions in the Middle East.

Iran’s army, meanwhile, said it had halted its strikes in the Gulf.

“Our strategy has essentially been retaliatory. We have also halted our retaliatory operations,” Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said, according to the AFP news agency.

However, like the US, Iran was also sure to maintain its bullish rhetoric, with Akraminia warning that the conflict would widen further if the US continues its attacks.

According to Turkiye’s Anadolu news agency, Pakistani and Qatari mediators have intensified communications with the US and Iran after both sides responded to a de-escalation formula to end the conflict.

Regarding the Omani delegation, Iran’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the talks about managing marine traffic in the Strait of Hormuz – the focus of the recent outbreak of hostilities – were “useful and progress was made”.

“Technical and political consultations” are ongoing, he added.

Meanwhile, incidents in the waterway, a key export route for oil and natural gas exports from the region, continued, maintaining the risk of escalation.

The US military’s Central Command said on Sunday that its naval blockade of Iran “remains in full effect”.

It noted that as of Saturday, it had redirected 12 commercial vessels, disabled two that had not complied with directions and boarded two “to ensure total compliance”.

Iranian media reported that Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps stopped six vessels from trying to transit the strait over the previous 24 hours by firing warning shots.

They also reported that an oil tanker exploded after hitting a mine in the strait. The Tasmin News Agency reported that the ship struck a mine after leaving the Iranian-approved route.

Control over the Strait of Hormuz is a point of contention between the US and Iran. Iran says it controls passage through the waterway under a memorandum of understanding that was signed by Washington and Tehran in June and established a 60-day period for the final terms of a deal to be negotiated.

The US says Iran does not control the strait and has tried to create a secondary route for vessels to transit the waterway.

title: ICE prepares major operation targeting Haitians losing TPS after Supreme Court ruling
excerpt: Heritage Foundation immigration director Lora Ries discusses a Haitian national charged in the alleged killing of a Pennsylvania state trooper. Fox News correspondent CB Cotton reports on ‘Fox Report....
body_text:
Heritage Foundation immigration director Lora Ries discusses a Haitian national charged in the alleged killing of a Pennsylvania state trooper. Fox News correspondent CB Cotton reports on ‘Fox Report.’

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to dramatically ramp up operations to locate and arrest Haitian nationals whose Temporary Protected Status (TPS) is expected to end imminently, multiple federal sources told Fox News.

The expanded operation is expected to begin as soon as this week.

The Supreme Court’s certified judgment is expected to be transmitted to the lower courts Monday, clearing the way for the Trump administration to proceed with ending TPS for more than 300,000 Haitians.

Federal sources told Fox News that Ohio will be heavily targeted because Springfield, Ohio, has a large Haitian population. ICE leadership has been notified of the operational plans, the sources said.

SUPREME COURT'S LATEST IMMIGRATION RULING WILL CAUSE AMERICANS TO 'DIE AND SUFFER' ATTORNEY WARNS

A sweeping ICE enforcement operation targeting Haitian migrants who are set to imminently lose their Temporary Protected Status is expected to begin as soon as this week, Fox News has learned. (Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)

Last month, the Supreme Court reversed lower-court judgments that had postponed the administration’s TPS terminations for Haiti and Syria while litigation continued.

TPS was first granted to Haiti following the country's devastating 2010 earthquake. The designation allows eligible foreign nationals from countries experiencing armed conflict, natural disasters or other extraordinary conditions to temporarily live and work legally in the United States.

SUPREME COURT WEIGHS TRUMP EFFORT TO TERMINATE TEMPORARY PROTECTIONS FOR HAITIAN, SYRIAN MIGRANTS

The anticipated operation follows the Trump administration's ongoing efforts to end Haiti's TPS designation. (Jaque Silva/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

The anticipated enforcement operation follows the Trump administration's long-running effort to end Haiti's TPS designation, arguing that the program was never intended to become a permanent form of legal status.

Following the Supreme Court's decision, White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson called the ruling "a tremendous win" for the administration.

"Today, the Supreme Court affirmed what President Trump has always maintained: temporary protected status is, by definition, temporary. It was never intended to be a pathway to permanent status or legal residency," Jackson told Fox News Digital. "The Trump Administration continues to lawfully end the egregious abuses to our immigration system that have hurt Americans for years."

Department of Homeland Security (DHS) General Counsel James Percival also praised the ruling in a post on X.

"The Court vindicates DHS yet again," Percival wrote. "The T in TPS stands for TEMPORARY, yet many of these designations became de facto amnesty. This is a win for the rule of law and common sense."

HOUSE REPUBLICANS MOVE TO MAKE TRUMP'S BORDER POLICIES PERMANENT

The anticipated enforcement operation comes as Springfield remains a focal point in the national immigration debate after the rapid growth of its Haitian community thrust the Ohio city into the national spotlight during the 2024 presidential campaign.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APPFox News has reached out to ICE and DHS for comment on the anticipated enforcement operation.

Fox News Digital's Alex Koch and Robert McGreevy contributed to this report.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Netanyahu accuses Mamdani of ‘fomenting hate’ in calls for PM’s arrest
excerpt:
Israeli prime minister says ICC’s war crime charges are ‘bogus’ and plans to be in New York for UN gathering this fall

Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday that Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, ...
body_text:
Israeli prime minister says ICC’s war crime charges are ‘bogus’ and plans to be in New York for UN gathering this fall

Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday that Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, is “fomenting hate” by calling the Israeli prime minister a war criminal who should be arrested over Israel’s war in Gaza if he visits the city for the United Nations general assembly.

Netanyahu said he intends to be in New York in September to address the annual UN gathering of world leaders, despite the mayor’s suggestion that he is not welcome. Mamdani said on Wednesday that while New York City does not have legal authority to execute an arrest warrant issued by the world’s top war crimes court, he encouraged the federal government to do so.

“He’s supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers – Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone,” Netanyahu said on the Fox News channel’s Sunday Morning Futures with Maria Bartiromo. “But he’s trying to turn one group against the other.”

The prime minister has become an increasingly polarizing figure over Israel’s war in Gaza, which was ignited by the 7 October 2023 deadly attack on southern Israel by Hamas militants. Israel also joined the US in starting the war against Iran on 28 February before launching a ground invasion in southern Lebanon in response to fire from the Iranian-backed Hezbollah group.

Netanyahu on Sunday dismissed the international criminal court (ICC)’s war crimes charges against him as “bogus”. He pointed to sexual misconduct allegations against the ICC’s top prosecutor, who was removed from that post on Friday, and said the warrant was an attempt to divert attention.

Mamdani’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Sunday.

Netanyahu on Sunday also said he was concerned that once-bipartisan political support for Israel in the US is at risk, particularly as progressive and far-left Democrats aligned with the Mamdani wing of the party splinter.

He also warned against rising antisemitism in the US and other western countries, saying that when he talks to people in New York City, home to the second-largest Jewish population in the world, “Jews feel very uncomfortable”.

“And I think it’s wrong,” he said. “The whole thing is wrong.”

Throughout his 2025 mayoral election campaign, Mamdani said he would seek to order the city’s police to execute the ICC’s arrest warrant over Netanyahu’s role in the war in Gaza.

“I want to be equally clear, Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large,” he said in his video message on Wednesday.

He told New Yorkers that he understood their frustration and that expressions of protest is something the city would “always respect”.

The Hague-based court has accused Netanyahu, his former defense minister and the late leader of Hamas of crimes against humanity. The Palestinian territory’s health ministry says more than 73,000 people have been killed in Israel’s offensive – roughly half of them women and children. About 1,200 people, most of them civilians, were killed in the initial Hamas attack on Israel.

Trump on Monday told Netanyahu in a social media post that he “will not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form, while in the United States of America”.

Netanyahu is expected in Washington DC on Monday to meet with Trump and attend funeral services for Lindsey Graham, the late Republican senator.

Graham, a leading defense hawk and strong supporter of Israel, died suddenly on 11 July of a likely torn aorta. Netanyahu called him a “great patriot” and one of Israel’s “greatest friends”.

title: Skipping sleep may pack on pounds faster than you think, new study finds
excerpt: During 'Fox & Friends' Wellness Week, sleep expert Dr. Rebecca Robbins analyzes popular sleep trends including melatonin, mouth taping, cooling pillows and sleep trackers. She explains melatonin's rol...
body_text:
During 'Fox & Friends' Wellness Week, sleep expert Dr. Rebecca Robbins analyzes popular sleep trends including melatonin, mouth taping, cooling pillows and sleep trackers. She explains melatonin's role in circadian rhythm, mouth taping benefits for nasal breathing and the importance of a 65-degree Fahrenheit sleep environment. Robbins advises adults aim for 7-9 hours of sleep per night for optimal health and longevity.

Regularly cutting back on sleep could cause the number on the scale to creep up, according to new research.

A study published in the Annals of Internal Medicine found that adults who got about 90 minutes less sleep each night for six weeks gained roughly one pound on average compared with periods when they got enough rest.

Researchers at Columbia University Irving Medical Center studied 95 adults who were already at risk for heart or metabolic disease, comparing six weeks of adequate sleep with six weeks of cutting about 90 minutes of sleep each night.

DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE

Regularly cutting back on sleep may cause the number on the scale to increase, a new study finds. (iStock)

By the end of the sleep-restricted phase, participants weighed about one pound more on average and had slightly larger waistlines. They also spent more time sitting, although their levels of moderate and vigorous exercise remained about the same.

While participants gained weight, researchers did not detect significant changes in body fat or muscle mass. They also did not track how much participants ate, so it's unclear what drove the increase.

Dr. Somi Javaid, an Ohio-based OB-GYN and founder of HerMD who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital that sleep plays an important role in regulating the body's metabolism.

Javaid said chronic sleep deprivation can make it harder for the body to regulate weight, but noted that women going through menopause may be especially vulnerable because sleep problems become more common during that stage of life.

"We are destroying women's sleep at the exact life stage when their metabolism is [the] least able to absorb the hit, then telling them to eat less and exercise more," Javaid said.

Adults gained about one pound on average and had slightly larger waistlines after six weeks of restricted sleep, compared with periods when they got enough rest. (iStock)

She added that the American Heart Association now recognizes sleep as one of its "Life's Essential 8" for heart health and recommends adults get seven to nine hours of sleep each night.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Chronic short sleep is not a lifestyle quirk," Javaid said. "We need to treat sleep as a vital sign of health."

While the findings suggest regularly getting less sleep may contribute to weight gain, the researchers noted several limitations of the study.

Experts say menopause can make it even harder for women to regulate their weight because sleep problems often become more common. (iStock)

They said the six-week study may not have been long enough to detect meaningful changes in body fat, which can take longer to develop than changes in body weight.

The researchers also noted that the study's relatively small sample size limited their ability to compare results among different groups of participants. In addition, some hormone measurements were collected only in the morning and may not have reflected fluctuations that occur throughout the day.

Kelly McGreal is a production assistant with the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

title: Cardinals end Jacoby Brissett contract dispute with deal worth up to $21M for 2026 season: reports
excerpt:
Carolina Panthers star edge rusher Nic Scourton reportedly tore his ACL late on a wet field during the team's practice this week. (This video contains AI-assisted content)

The pay raise quarterback J...
body_text:
Carolina Panthers star edge rusher Nic Scourton reportedly tore his ACL late on a wet field during the team's practice this week. (This video contains AI-assisted content)

The pay raise quarterback Jacoby Brissett was looking for was finally given to him by the Arizona Cardinals.

Unlike most hold-ins/hold-outs, Brissett wasn’t looking for a new extension from his club, but rather a raise heading into the 2026 NFL season where he figures to be the starting quarterback. He was set to make $4.88 million as his base salary.

Now, Brissett is set to make $15.5 million in base pay for 2026, according to multiple reports. The new 2026 contract could also get up to $21 million with incentives.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Jacoby Brissett No. 7 of the Arizona Cardinals warms up prior to a game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, Ohio, on Dec. 28, 2025. (Getty Images)

This stalemate between the journeyman quarterback and the Cardinals sparked some debate over whether it was even right that Brissett was asking for a raise.

But following the release of Kyler Murray , who eventually signed with the Minnesota Vikings, Brissett was in line to be a starter, and he wished to be paid accordingly. His new deal isn’t remotely close to top starter money, however, Brissett appears happy to finally get to common ground.

PATRICK MAHOMES LEAPS PAST DAK PRESCOTT AS NFL'S HIGHEST-PAID QB WITH RECORD CHIEFS EXTENSION WORTH $504.75M

Brissett chose not to participate in the Cardinals’ spring workouts, though he did report to training camp on time. Because of the latter decision, it was expected he and the Cardinals would reach a deal soon.

It’s yet another regime change for the Cardinals, with Mike LaFleur assuming the head coach role left vacant after the firing of Jonathan Gannon. Brissett sits atop the depth chart after the Murray cut, while Arizona drafted Miami quarterback Carson Beck and signed Gardner Minshew II for competition at training camp.

Jacoby Brissett of the Arizona Cardinals looks on during mandatory minicamp at Dignity Health Arizona Cardinals Training Center in Tempe, Ariz., on June 9, 2026. (Getty Images)

Brissett took over starting duties during the 2025 season after Murray suffered a foot injury. It wasn’t soon before Brissett was operating the Cardinals’ offense more efficiently than his injured teammate, with players like tight end Trey McBride and wide receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. seeing an uptick in their own stat lines.

Brissett is scheduled for free agency after this season, but perhaps he can remain in good favor with the Cardinals with another good year. The offense around him was also bolstered, especially with Notre Dame running back Jeremiyah Love being drafted third overall back in April.

Brissett has been working out with his teammates to begin training camp, including newcomers like Love, but he hasn’t been participating in 11-on-11 sessions of practice. That should change now after the raise agreement.

But the pay raise doesn’t necessarily mean Brissett is guaranteed the starting role come Week 1 against the Los Angeles Chargers. He will have to earn that spot over Minshew and Beck, though he has the rapport necessary with the team’s top pass game options to think he will do just that.

Jacoby Brissett No. 7 of the Arizona Cardinals passes the ball during a game against the Los Angeles Rams at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, Calif., on Jan. 4, 2026. (Getty Images)

The Cardinals and Carolina Panthers were the first full teams to report to training camp, as the new season truly gets underway. The rest of the league will have their veterans arriving on July 28, making this the week where position battles take flight across the NFL.

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Former President Hernandez returns to Honduras after Trump pardon
excerpt:
Former President Juan Orlando Hernandez has returned to Honduras from the United States after President Donald Trump pardoned him after he received a 45-year jail sentence for drug trafficking.

Herna...
body_text:
Former President Juan Orlando Hernandez has returned to Honduras from the United States after President Donald Trump pardoned him after he received a 45-year jail sentence for drug trafficking.

Hernandez returned to the Central American country on Sunday, four years after being extradited to the US. He is now due to go on trial in Honduras on fraud and money-laundering charges, but activists worry that he will not face real justice.

Trump granted Hernandez a presidential pardon in December, asserting that he did not receive a fair trial and was set up by former US President Joe Biden’s administration.

“I cannot deny the profound emotion and joy I feel in my heart to be returning home,” Hernandez wrote on social media earlier this month, saying he was counting down the days to see his family.

“It wasn’t easy. The process has been extremely difficult … and what I experienced in prison, I truly wouldn’t wish on anyone,” he added.

As he arrived at Palmerola International Airport, he was greeted by his family and dozens of supporters of his National Party.

Despite his pardon on the US charges, Hernandez is expected to appear in court on August 3 to face the Honduran charges.

However, he was not detained upon arrival in Honduras because an arrest warrant was suspended in June, and local activists are concerned that the trial will turn out to be a sham.

“Everything points to the suspension being the first step,” said Joaquin Mejia, a lawyer and researcher for the Reflection, Research and Communication Team, a human rights organisation.

“He’ll come, they’ll likely issue him alternative measures to imprisonment to keep up appearances, and then he’ll end up without any problem, without any sanction.”

“There is a social majority that is outraged but doesn’t speak out because of fear,” Mejia added “We’re talking about the boss of all drug bosses.”

Hernandez, once considered an ally by the US in its “war on drugs”, led Honduras from 2014 to 2022. During that time, he said during a meeting with drug dealers that they would “shove the drugs right up the noses of the gringos”, according to a US prosecutor at his trial in New York.

A Pandora Papers corruption investigation accused Hernandez and other high-profile officials of diverting nearly $11m in state funds to political campaigns from 2010 to 2013. Some of this money was allegedly used for Hernandez’s first presidential campaign.

Former President Porfirio Lobo and ex-Finance Minister Wilfredo Cerrato were both implicated in the same investigation, and the charges against them were dismissed.

excerpt:

body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

At least one person was killed, and six others were injured after gunfire erupted at a massive party in rural California Saturday night, sending hundreds of attendees scrambling for safety, authorities said.

The incident unfolded shortly after 10 p.m. local time in Morgan Hill, about 25 miles south of San Jose, according to the Santa Clara County Sheriff's Office.

Authorities said the gathering was an unsanctioned party promoted on social media that drew more than 300 attendees.

GUNFIRE SHATTERS TORONTO LATIN STREET FESTIVAL, LEAVING AT LEAST 2 DEAD AND MULTIPLE WOUNDED

FILE - A shooting erupted in Morgan Hill, California, about 25 miles south of San Jose, on July 25, 2026, prompting San Jose police to respond to the scene. (KTVU)

Deputies initially responded to reports of intoxicated people in the road and someone throwing bottles at passing vehicles, but arrived to find the party in chaos after gunfire erupted, according to the sheriff's office.

Responding deputies provided lifesaving aid until emergency medical personnel arrived, but one person was pronounced dead at the scene.

Officials said multiple others suffered gunshot wounds and were rushed to local hospitals.

GUNMAN CHARGED AFTER WOUNDING 9 IN TUCSON NIGHTLIFE SHOOTING BEFORE COP TAKES HIM DOWN

FILE - The Anderson Lake is seen in unincorporated Morgan Hill, California, on Aug. 8, 2022. Authorities are investigating a deadly shooting at an unsanctioned Morgan Hill party that drew more than 300 attendees. (Li Jianguo/Xinhua)

Preliminary information indicates the suspect used a handgun, though no suspects have been publicly identified.

Homicide detectives said they believe the shooting was an isolated incident and noted the investigation is expected to be "lengthy and complex."

"This tragic and senseless violence is entirely unacceptable," Santa Clara County Sheriff Robert Jonsen said in a statement. "Our hearts go out to the victim's family, those recovering from their injuries and everyone in our community affected by this traumatic event."

"We will work tirelessly until those responsible for this horrific act are identified, apprehended, and held fully accountable," Jonsen added.

FILE - Multiple law enforcement agencies responded after a shooting erupted in Morgan Hill, California, on July 25, 2026, leaving one person dead and six others injured. (DAVID PASHAEE/Middle East Images/AFP)

Officials said multiple agencies responded to the scene, including the Morgan Hill Police Department, Gilroy Police Department, California Highway Patrol and San Jose Police Department.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Morgan Hill Police Department, Gilroy Police Department, California Highway Patrol and San Jose Police Department for more information.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital
