title: I grew up near Andy Burnham. This is what shaped our new PM
excerpt:
In the Warrington suburb of Culcheth, people are hopeful about what one of their own can achieve as the first northern PM in half a century

The Cherry Tree pub is an unassuming local. On a busy road ...
body_text:
In the Warrington suburb of Culcheth, people are hopeful about what one of their own can achieve as the first northern PM in half a century

The Cherry Tree pub is an unassuming local. On a busy road in the Cheshire village of Culcheth, it is a chain-run pub where four shots cost £8, every burger comes with a soft drink, and sport is shown all day on the big screens. It is also a favourite of Andy Burnham, the new prime minister.

Many of the drinkers have a story about – arguably – Culcheth’s most famous son.

“I was at school with Andy,” says Mike Hodgson. “He went to our school, he likes the Smiths … He’s got a good northern sense of person, and he’s done a good job in Manchester.”

Janice Fox chips in: “I used to play with him when we were kids.”

The Cherry is in the opening scene of Burnham’s book Head North. One night in April 1989, in its smoke-filled back room, the future leader of the country is recovering from a bout of “impostor syndrome” while home from Cambridge University. Panic, by the Smiths, is playing on the jukebox.

It is also a place I know well: like Burnham, I grew up in this quiet Warrington suburb halfway between Manchester and Liverpool, I have spent many nights at the Cherry, and like many locals, I have my own story about him.

Here is mine: 15 years ago I met the then Labour MP for Leigh while drinking with mates in the Cherry. Labour had recently lost the 2010 election, and Burnham had recently lost to Ed Miliband in the race to lead the party in opposition. Home from London for the weekend, I was struggling to get a job, so plucked up the courage for a chat.

As the then shadow education secretary, he talked me through the impact of the Conservatives’ plan to cut Labour’s Building Schools for the Future programme. That £55bn landmark New Labour policy turned cold, leaky 1960s prefab schools around the country into modern buildings of which teachers and pupils could be proud; it rebuilt my secondary, Culcheth high school.

He gave me his mobile number and invited me for a cup of tea in parliament. I expected to be ghosted. But a few weeks later we were sitting in SW1 picking up the conversation over a brew in Portcullis House. Burnham told me Britain’s media and political landscape needed more northern accents like ours.

On Friday, Burnham opened No 10 North, in Manchester; a first step in his promise to rebalance power away from Westminster to deliver “good growth in every postcode”.

This week I travelled back to WA3 to find out what people make of Burnham becoming the first northern prime minister since Harold Wilson 50 years ago. He has spoken with pride of his roots, and how reversing the decimation of Britain’s industrial communities under Margaret Thatcher is a top priority.

Outside the Cherry, one group of friends say it’s at least nice that someone local is in No 10. One of the women lifts her sunglasses and we are transported back a quarter of a century: it’s my old geography teacher, Mrs Crinion.

“I was quite proud seeing him walking down the street,” says one of her friends. “I felt a bit chuffed. I hope he does a good job.” But does having one of our own in high office change anything? “I very much doubt it,” says another.

Earlier this month, Burnham recorded a video for social media arriving “home” from London at Warrington Bank Quay train station. It is far from the most beautiful spot on the railway, in the shadow of an old Unilever soap factory that is up for demolition.

Once the diggers have finished here there are plans for an AI datacentre – a fact deployed by Keir Starmer last month as a symbol of how a “left behind” community could reinvent itself.

But this description elides much of Warrington’s character. The town has its difficulties – not least the boarded-up shops and crumbling, shuttered nightclubs on Bridge Street – but it is more affluent than many other “red wall” communities in this pocket of north-west England.

As a postwar new town, there are miles of suburbia stretching into the Cheshire countryside. There are good transport links, affordable housing, and opportunities for work in high-paying sectors, such as technology and nuclear energy.

This year, the Centre for Cities thinktank suggested Britain could do with a few more towns like Warrington: local disposable incomes have galloped ahead here, growing 2.2 times faster than the UK average since 2013. Perhaps this could influence the Burnham economic blueprint?

Still, many locals feel let down by Labour. Before Burnham replaced Starmer, Reform was predicted to sweep away the party in Warrington’s two constituencies. But many say the new prime minister’s background could help change things.

John Cross, whose family has run a butcher’s stall in Warrington market for five generations, is among them: “I’m made up. That we’ve got someone from the north, rather than someone from down south. There needs to be more balance, how we’re governed in this country. Don’t get me wrong; he’s got an absolute job in front of him. But I think it’s a good thing [that Burnham is prime minister].”

Support is, however, far from uniform, including in Culcheth. Sitting outside McDee’s cafe, Tom says he has little time for politicians – “all a bunch of thieves”. Net zero, failure to invest in defence and prosecutions of British soldiers are his complaints. “It’s Labour, isn’t it? I don’t believe any of them will do anything different.”

Inside the cafe, others are more positive. Veysel Hazar, the manager, seats me at the table where he has served Burnham and his mother, Eileen. He does not do politics, but says of the new prime minister: “Amazing person. I’m happy for Culcheth.”

Eating lunch on the table opposite, the Ollerton family are from nearby Golborne – where Burnham now lives and where coal mining once dominated. They have seen him out running in his retro Everton shirt, and are friends with his nextdoor neighbour on a road a few streets from his new Makerfield constituency.

“You knew he was going to win. Makerfield would have voted Reform if it wasn’t for him,” says Marilyn Ollerton.

“He’s very relatable, rather than just being somebody on the television; somebody from down south that you’ve probably got nothing in common with,” says Lianne Ollerton.

Some places in Warrington – particularly the terraced streets near the town’s old wire factories – rank among the most deprived in England. Burnham’s former Leigh constituency, and his Makerfield one, are among them. Culcheth, though, is seen as “posh”.

Where Burnham grew up, on Common Lane, many homes have gated driveways and easily sell for more than £1m. Locals jokingly call the area “Upper Culcheth” to distinguish it from the rest of the village, including the postwar social housing estate built for officers at the nearby Risley prison.

There is a golf course, parades of neat shops, a butcher, hair and beauty salons and pubs, as well as two Italian restaurants, both of which I worked in as a teenager.

The presence of SUVs and flash cars has steadily increased – in part the spillover from Manchester’s economic renaissance. I do not remember Culcheth being this affluent. It was comfortable, but not in the same league as the footballer-belt Cheshire villages south of Warrington.

But while it does not fit the media stereotype of Coronation Street-style terrace housing, flat caps and spoil heaps, it is still within touching distance of the industrial decline that has crushed this region.

Growing up, the legacy of industry was obvious. I saw the demolition of Parkside colliery’s concrete winding towers – the last deep mine in the Lancashire coalfield – from my bedroom window. A decade earlier, Burnham would pass here on his bus to school – St Aelreds Catholic technology college, now renamed Hope academy, in Newton-le-Willows – and bang on its window to show support to the picket line at the colliery gates during the 1984 miners’ strike.

Born in 1970 at Aintree hospital in Liverpool, Burnham moved from Merseyside to Culcheth at about age one, after his father, Roy, was promoted to a job in Manchester. An engineer at the Post Office, he had once worked at a telephone exchange in the village – opposite the Cherry Tree – and liked the feel of the place.

Raised Catholic, Burnham went to St Lewis primary school, a short walk down Mustard Lane from Croft primary, where I went. He recalls in Head North a “modest” upbringing. There were no holidays abroad. But his family also “didn’t want for anything”, and he went on to study at Cambridge, where he met his future wife, Dutch-born Marie-France van Heel.

Burnham is often in the village playing five-a-side football with his brothers, who are teachers, and their friends, including relatives of another famous son of Culcheth, Roger Hunt, the Liverpool striker and England 1966 World Cup winner.

In the Lords of the North barbershop in Warrington town centre, hairdresser Nicole Egan tells me Burnham’s brother John taught her at school. “If he’s anything like his brother … 10 out of 10. Top family. I’m made up. He seems to be doing some great things already.”

Egan’s mother, Cheryl Good, is cutting a boy’s hair. She says the prime minister went out with her old boss back “when he was a raver” in an Adidas tracksuit.

“He went to a normal school. He wasn’t privately educated where they were told they were special or better than anybody else. So he’s started from the same starting point as everybody else, and he’s done really well for himself.”

Both are Green voters but see Burnham as moving in the right direction, despite hearing “alarm bells” over the rumours that he could allow more North Sea oil and gas drilling. But first impressions matter: addressing the cost of living has cut through in a way that locals say has raised their hopes.

“Working families are struggling,” says Egan. “So the things he’s done at the moment – the [cutting of the] tax on electricity bills, £2 cap on the fares on buses, and that’s only in his first couple of days. I’m very hopeful – what little we have left of that”

Burnham was in Culcheth after a regular football game with his brothers, in his first fortnight as the mayor of Greater Manchester, when he was told of the Manchester Arena bombing on 22 May 2017. It was a moment that would become a turning point for the city, and for Burnham.

People are full of praise for his ability to empathise. Three years ago, Burnham was at the candlelight vigil in his home village for Brianna Ghey, the 16-year-old transgender girl murdered in Culcheth Linear Park.

They also credit him for the economic turnaround of the city along the M62. Manchester – and its resulting “ism” – is central to Burnham’s political and economic blueprint for Britain; founded in the coordination of the private and public sector, and helped by new powers for local areas through devolution.

Grabbing power from Westminster and Whitehall resonates in these parts.

In the market, Neil Kelly, who leads community engagement for the local rugby league team, Warrington Wolves, is having a coffee with his colleague Adam Leah. “There’s been a lot of fights with Whitehall all of the time. So I think devolution is going to work in that sense for Warrington.

“You’ll see for Warrington what it means, and how it can have a real effect, particularly around on the streets and the towns, and the cultures and the communities.”

There are, however, tensions and undercurrents. Warrington is among the most heavily indebted councils in England, with an outstanding pile worth more than £1.5bn. The town’s Labour leadership argues it needed to borrow to invest, to offset Tory austerity directed from Westminster. But critics fear handing over more powers might not be the right answer.

The bus network in Warrington could also show the opportunities and difficulties of local power. Unlike most places, the town never lost control of its buses in the wave of 1980s privatisation.

Buses have long been a Burnham preoccupation, after he overhauled the network in Greater Manchester. The region’s Bee Network, a system of joined-up, accessible transport, has brought buses under local control through franchising. In Warrington, the neon yellow fleet – close in colour to its Manchester equivalent – is fully electric, and locally controlled, but more expensive than many would like, at £5.90 for a day ticket.

In Culcheth there will be tensions with Labour’s national priorities on housing development; in a semi-rural community ringed by green-belt land, many do not want to see more homes built, despite the climbing house prices pushing young people away.

Still, at a Labour party branch meeting at Culcheth library, there is hope that Burnham can square the circle because he knows these issues. Margaret Webber, the branch chair, and Matt Smith, a local Labour councillor who was once my high school form tutor, say that where the person who leads Britain is from has an important bearing.

“He’s got a lot of good will behind him, because he’s saying what a lot of people think.”

title: Reclaiming stolen childhoods: swimming classes resume in Gaza after three years of war
excerpt:
In sea pools built with sandbags and rubble, Amjed Tantesh gives traumatised children brief respite from their daily lives

Swimming classes have started again in Gaza after three years of war, with h...
body_text:
In sea pools built with sandbags and rubble, Amjed Tantesh gives traumatised children brief respite from their daily lives

Swimming classes have started again in Gaza after three years of war, with hundreds of children learning to float, doggy paddle and take their first strokes in five makeshift sea pools built from sandbags and rubble.

The lessons allow a few hundred girls and boys to reclaim their childhood for a few hours in a place where there are no playgrounds, no formal education and children live in fear of continuing Israeli attacks. A UN survey in March found that 96% of children felt death was imminent.

“Swimming gives me a chance to escape the war, and the worries I live with,” said Alma Shabat, 13, who saw her mother killed in an Israeli strike in May.

After three weeks of classes, her favourite stroke is freestyle, she has made new friends and she is no longer afraid of the waves and open sea. “Coming to the beach is a beautiful and enjoyable experience,” she said.

Amjed Tantesh, who founded Gaza’s first swimming academy more than two decades ago, has mobilised dozens of volunteers this summer to create the string of pools on the beaches of central Gaza, with tarpaulins providing some shade from the fierce Mediterranean sun.

There is very little heavy machinery left in Gaza so they did everything by hand, moving tonnes of rubble and filling sandbags to build walls, then excavating sand to deepen the pools.

In the morning they hold free classes for children whose parents were killed in Israeli attacks. In the afternoon, the pools are open to everyone and constantly filled with delighted children splashing in the warm water.

Tulin Al-Othmaneh, 10, and Aseel Al-Kafarna

“Its a rare chance to enjoy, relax and reclaim part of their stolen childhood,” said Tantesh, who has also worked as a journalist for the Guardian and other outlets. His niece, Seham Tantesh, reports for the Guardian from Gaza. “The pools attract children from all along the beach like huge magnets”.

Most Palestinian children have endured years of extreme trauma. There is the loss and maiming of loved ones, with one in ten of the prewar population killed or injured in Israeli attacks. Thousands more are thought to be buried under the rubble.

A big group of the children pose for a photo on the beach

Children form a chain before getting into the water

Gaza has the highest concentration of child amputees in the world. “Disability among Palestinian children has ceased to be an individual medical condition and has now become a defining demographic reality,” a UN commission said in a report on Israel’s targeting of Palestinian children.

The human-made famine caused by Israel’s siege last year will leave some children with lifelong mental and physical stunting.

Instructor Ali Al-Attar with a group of the children

There has been no formal schooling for three years, and almost all school buildings have been damaged or destroyed. There are nearly 700,000 school-age children in Gaza, and only a minority have access to the makeshift tent schools run by aid groups.

Survivors are crammed into crowded, hot and noisy tent camps in just a third of the prewar Gaza without adequate water or sanitation.

Amjed Tantesh takes a selfie while a swimming class takes place behind him

Swimming classes are a desperately needed escape from this grim reality, physically and mentally. “Being here allows me to train, play and breath fresh air, away from the tents,” said Maryam al Musri, 10, who lost her father in the war.

Laila Qahman, 14, who lost her seven-year-old brother when a mosque near where he was playing was bombed and who dreams of becoming a pharmacist, said swimming gave her the chance to relax, cool down and forget about life in a tent.

“I come here every other day because it makes me feel like I’m living my life and enjoying my time, instead of staying in the tent listening to the sounds of shelling and living with fear and sadness,” she said.

“Before I learned how to swim, I was a little afraid of the sea and did not have the courage to go into the water. Now, I feel much more confident and no longer feel afraid when I swim.”

So far 700 children have attended six weeks of classes, and Tantesh hopes to teach thousands more over the summer if he can get funding to pay teachers, who are currently all working for free, and cover other basic expenses.

The joy of these young swimmers has been healing for him as well, as he mourns his older brother Bahjat, a karate champion killed in an Israeli attack last year as the brothers fled their family home under Israeli evacuation orders.

“Bahjat was the one that taught me swimming in the first place, then inspired me to pursue sporting excellence as a young man,” he said. “To have him die in my arms was the worst thing imaginable.”

A group of children sitting on the beach after their swimming class

The original academy was inspired in equal measure by hope and tragedy. Palestine made its Olympic debut at the Atlanta Games in 1996, giving athletes from Gaza the first chance to compete on the world’s biggest stage, and Tantesh a new mission.

“I wanted to be at the Olympics, but I started as a professional swimmer at a very late age. So I decided to achieve my dream through a new generation,” he said.

Closer to home, each summer brought deaths by drowning at sea. Families would flock to the beach to relax, splash around and cool off but few people could swim and there were no lifeguards at his local beach. Swimming lessons would make children safer and they could train future lifeguards, he decided.

Kamal Taha, 12, being interviewed by a local TV channel

His biggest challenge when the classes first launched was persuading parents to sign up their children. “People were terrified by water, the sea looked like a monster to them as it consumed dozens of people annually,” he said.

For the first few years children learned to swim in Gaza’s port, where breakwaters protected children from the waves. Then he constructed a series of pools along the coast for classes, where about 11,000 people learned to swim.

The biggest, built with rubble from homes bombed by Israel in 2014, was more than 1,000 square metres. Israeli attacks since 2023 razed all the pools, killed tens of swimming students and at least six coaches, and injured countless more.

Restarting classes seemed almost impossible. “I only had the sea, but the sea is dangerous even during summer. You have jellyfish, you have high waves, strong currents, rocks,” he said.

So he came up with the plan for new pools, for the sake of Gaza’s children and as a tribute to his brother. Seeing the children leave the horrors of war behind for a brief period, when they dive into the sea, has also been healing for him.

“Actually the first person I helped with this project was myself,” he said. “It has given me a great feeling of happiness and recovery. I am alive again.”

You can find more about the swimming pool project here

title: UK’s largest Muslim event goes ahead with added security as hate crime rises
excerpt:
Jalsa Salana in Hampshire has had enhanced support from police, emergency services and local authorities

Security has been increased by several hundred additional staff at the UK’s largest Muslim con...
body_text:
Jalsa Salana in Hampshire has had enhanced support from police, emergency services and local authorities

Security has been increased by several hundred additional staff at the UK’s largest Muslim convention, Jalsa Salana, alongside enhanced coordination with police, emergency services and local authorities, against a backdrop of growing anti-Muslim sentiment.

Last month, another big Islamic gathering was forced to close early after 12 people were arrested, including three on suspicion of conspiracy to murder, over a suspected far-right threat.

Did Jalsa Salana’s organisers think twice about going ahead?

“Not once. Not for a second,” said Rafiq Hayat, the head of the UK chapter of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community, which organises the festival.

Now in its 60th year, Jalsa Salana is expected to draw about 50,000 people from more than 100 countries to a temporary site in Hampshire this weekend. The convention opened on Friday with prayers, speeches – including an address from the community’s global leader, Hazrat Mirza Masroor Ahmad – and the raising of a union jack at the centre of the 208-acre site. MPs, bishops and other public figures are expected to attend.

Hayat says the community has weathered hostility before. The Ahmadiyya Muslim Community has been in Britain for more than a century, having established itself in 1913, and built one of London’s first purpose-built mosques in 1926.

“I personally have been in London since 1967, so I have been through all of the various rightwing movements: from skinheads, to the ‘rivers of blood’ speech by Enoch Powell to the British National party. We have seen it all,” Hayat said.

During the construction of the movement’s mosque in Morden in the 1990s, hundreds of British National party supporters protested outside planning meetings, he added.

But rather than withdrawing, Hayat said, the community deliberately invested in relationships with its neighbours.

“We created a liaison group,” Hayat said. “We invited people from the church and from various local groups, from the local authority to the police. And we said we would hold a meeting every month at our mosque, and appointed a local councillor as the chair of the meeting.”

He added that the first two meetings were “very heated”. But, 30 years later, “they will not do anything without us being involved”.

For Hayat, that experience provides a useful lesson to how to respond to this current climate of rising anti-Muslim hatred. Latest figures show that one mosque is attacked in Britain every five days, while anti-Muslim hate crime in England and Wales rose by 19% in the 12 months to March 2025.

“One of the things that the community has been doing over the last 60 years is to bring people of all faith, all backgrounds, all ethnicities, everyone, together,” Hayat said. “The founder of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community reminded us that true Muslims should embody the teaching of the holy prophet Muhammad – that loyalty to the country in which you live is an integral part of your faith.”

But hostility towards the Ahmadiyya community does not come solely from the far right. Ahmadis have long faced persecution from extremist Muslims, both abroad, particularly in Pakistan and, at times, in Britain.

In 2016, Asad Shah, an Ahmadi Muslim man, was killed outside his shop in Glasgow by another Muslim in a religiously motivated murder.

“The saddest part is that it is sometimes easier to deal with the rightwing than with some Muslim extremists,” Hayat said. “I grew up with lots of Muslims. Some of my closest friends are Muslims who are not Ahmadi. But there are some who have very extreme views.

“But when we have these conferences, lots of Muslims come. When we had the big iftar at our large mosque, about 60% were young Muslims who weren’t Ahmadi.”

Hayat said the community’s answer to threats was not to retreat from public life but to become more visible.

“We say to our children that they must not be embarrassed about being Muslim in this country,” he said. “These misconceptions about Islam have to be dealt with. And this is what I say to the larger Muslim community: please engage with people.”

He didn’t minimise the level of threat facing the Muslim community, pointing to a recent incident in which one of their mosques was attacked, while hatred against Muslims had become increasingly visible online.

Yet, he passionately believes that personal encounters remain the most effective antidote.

Hayat recalled one visitor who admitted she had shared her live location with her husband before visiting the mosque, telling him that if he did not hear from her every 15 minutes, he should come to get her.

Afterwards, she told Hayat she found warmth at the mosque and wanted to return with her family.

“You don’t see my colour any more. You see the human being behind it. This is the key to peaceful coexistence,” Hayat said.

title: UK savings deals: the heat is on as banks offer up to 8%
excerpt:
Don’t delay in taking advantage of the competition that is pushing up interest rates and increasing choice, experts say

It is shaping up to be a decent summer for savers as fierce competition among p...
body_text:
Don’t delay in taking advantage of the competition that is pushing up interest rates and increasing choice, experts say

It is shaping up to be a decent summer for savers as fierce competition among providers pushes up interest rates and increases choice.

You can currently get instant- and easy-access accounts that pay up to 5% interest, and fixed-rate savings bonds that pay almost that much. Meanwhile, those looking for a regular savings account can now get up to 8%.

So if you have cash languishing in a savings, or current, account that is earning no interest, or only giving you a paltry return, now is the time to move it to a better-paying home.

“Things are looking promising – the choice is really good, but it’s all about being proactive and switching, and making the most of these products while they are there,” says Rachel Springall at the financial data provider Moneyfacts.

This month, the number of “live” savings accounts paying more than the Bank of England base rate – currently 3.75% – rose to 1,385, the highest figure for more than six years, says Moneyfacts. That figure represents more than half of the total number. (Though it is based on the interest rate paid on a balance of £5,000.)

With the cost of living still a big issue, many savers will be keen to keep their cash close at hand where they can get at it if needed. The average non-Isa easy-access account rate is now the highest it has been for almost a year, at 2.53%.

The top-paying easy-access accounts offer quite a bit more.

Revolut, the fast-growing fintech that is now a fully fledged bank, recently launched a “market-leading” savings rate offer for new UK customers. If you open one of its instant-access savings accounts between now and 4 August, you can benefit from a rate of 5% until 4 December this year. This will apply on balances up to £25,000. After 4 December, the interest will revert to the rate determined by your plan. So if you are on Revolut’s free standard plan, or its £3.99-a-month Plus plan, for example, it will fall to 2.9%.

Chase, the British retail arm of the US bank JP Morgan, has an easy-access account called Chase Saver that pays new customers 4.5%. That rate is boosted by a 2.25% interest bonus that lasts for 12 months – the account’s standard rate is 2.25%. It lets people stash away up to £3m – however, a (free) Chase current account is required.

Fixed-rate savings bonds offer some of the highest rates. You typically have to tie up your money for between six months and five years, and they provide a clear, guaranteed return.

One-year fixed-rate bonds have been “very popular”, says Springall, as many people do not want to tie up their cash for too long. The good news is that this month, the average one-year fixed bond rate rose to 4.22% – its highest since November 2024.

However, at the time of writing you could get more than that: for example, Marcus by Goldman Sachs had a one-year fixed-rate bond paying 4.9%. Up to £250,000 can be paid into this online account. And Atom Bank has a one-year fixed-rate bond paying 4.8%.

Regular savings accounts often offer eye-catching interest rates. With these, you put aside some money each month for a limited period. Often, you have to have a current account with the bank offering the product, and in many cases the headline rate only lasts for a year.

Lloyds launched a new instant-access regular savings account earlier this month called Monthly Saver. The account pays an impressive 8%. There is also a version available for customers of Halifax and Bank of Scotland, although the Halifax one (called Regular Saver) does not let you access your savings during the 12-month term. In all cases you can save from £25 to £250 a month by standing order or bank transfer, and your interest is paid 12 months after you open the account.

Santander also has a regular savings account paying 8% for 12 months. It lets you save up to £200 a month from its current accounts.

But watch out for the savings interest “tax trap” if you are putting a large-ish sum of money into a decent-paying non-Isa account.

Interest earned outside an Isa is subject to tax once you go over your personal savings allowance. This is £1,000 for basic-rate taxpayers and £500 for higher-rate taxpayers, and up to £5,000 if you earn less than £17,570 a year.

title: Herbicide banned in 70 countries to be pulled from sale in Australia by chemical maker
excerpt:
Syngenta says it will stop selling paraquat in Australia after new regulations on chemical linked to Parkinson’s disease

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Syngenta, the pro...
body_text:
Syngenta says it will stop selling paraquat in Australia after new regulations on chemical linked to Parkinson’s disease

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Syngenta, the producer of a herbicide banned in more than 70 countries and which has been linked to Parkinson’s disease, will stop selling paraquat in Australia, saying new regulations has made it “commercially unviable”.

The decision to pull the product follows new restrictions on the highly poisonous chemical announced by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority in June.

Paraquat has been produced by the Swiss company for decades, but has long been linked to Parkinson’s disease in users.

It is banned in more than 70 countries and has been prohibited in the European Union since 2007.

It cannot be used in domestic settings in Australia, but is still widely used in agriculture, particularly broad-acre cropping like grains, sugarcane and cotton. The APVMA assessed that the weight of evidence does not show that paraquat exposure through approved uses increases the risk of developing Parkinson’s disease.

But it did impose new restrictions to address acute exposure and risks to animals.

The company said the decision to pull the products followed a commercial review carried out in the wake of the APVMA’s rules.

Syngenta ANZ’s managing director, David Van Ryswyk, said the company will manage the phase-out of its paraquat products in strict alignment with the APVMA’s designated sell-out and use-by timelines.

“Regulatory constraints, combined with a highly complex and increasingly expensive supply chain, have made the paraquat herbicide products commercially unviable,” Van Ryswyk said.

The new restrictions on the herbicide required that backpack sprayers be phased out, mandate additional personal protective equipment for users and set a much lower maximum rate of application per hectare.

At the time of the APVMA’s decision, Syngenta said the pesticide “does not cause an unacceptable environmental impact” and that the regulation would limit its use in a significant number of crop use cases.

The company had planned to continue supplying through a third-party manufacturer, but on Friday it said the new regulations and an increasingly expensive supply chain had made the product unviable.

Generic paraquat products will still be available for local farmers.

Last month, the Melbourne neurologist Associate Prof Wes Thevathasan told the ABC that there has been “global consensus” in his field that exposure to paraquat was linked to the development of Parkinson’s disease.

“There are now multiple epidemiological studies or real-world exposure studies that have suggested that paraquat increases the risk of Parkinson’s disease by around threefold,” Thevathasan said.

Grain Producers Australia spokesperson Andrew Weidemann said Syngenta’s decision created uncertainty for local growers.

“Its withdrawal leaves some important questions about what happens next,” he said.

“Australia is a relatively small market, and decisions like this call future investment into question.

“If companies cannot see sufficient value in maintaining products here, growers risk being left with fewer choices at the same time we urgently need more tools to manage herbicide resistance.”

title: Saudi Arabia and Houthis exchange fire as US attacks tanker in Hormuz Strait
excerpt:
A vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman

Saudi Arabia launched airstrikes on Houthi targets in the Yemeni port city of Hodeida and a nearby island on Friday, after the Iran-backe...
body_text:
A vessel in the Strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman

Saudi Arabia launched airstrikes on Houthi targets in the Yemeni port city of Hodeida and a nearby island on Friday, after the Iran-backed group announced a maritime blockade and attacked Saudi ships.

Saudi authorities later issued emergency alerts for the province of Jizan as the Houthis claimed responsibility for a missile attack on the city of Jizan.

Early on Saturday, the Houthis' Ansarollah media said on Telegram that a "Yemeni missile strike" had caused fires in the Saudi city of Jizan.

Meanwhile in the Strait of Hormuz, the US military said on Friday it had fired on and disabled a tanker ship in the Gulf of Oman that was attempting to evade the American blockade on Iranian ports.

The vessel attacked by the US is the second commercial ship the US has disabled since it reimposed its blockade earlier this month.

"We disabled the tanker after the crew attempted to run the blockade at least four times prior," Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, spokesman for US Central Command, told AFP.

"The crew was repeatedly warned, didn't comply, and US forces on scene disabled the ship after firing into its engine room," he said. "The ship is no longer transiting to Iran."

Earlier, a delegation from Oman arrived in Iran's capital Tehran for talks on the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's state-run IRNA news agency reported. Oman controls the strait's southern coastline.

The US and Iran have traded fire for almost two weeks, with Iran on Friday saying it had carried out drone strikes on US military facilities and bases across the Middle East in retaliation for the 13th consecutive night of American attacks on the country.

Speaking to reporters at the White House on Friday afternoon, Trump continued to threaten further attacks while saying that negotiations were continuing.

"We are talking to them. I think they're being serious. I think ... they are being by far the most serious that we've seen them, but that doesn't mean we get there," he said.

Asked about his exit strategy for the Iran war, Trump said: "There's a military exit where we just keep going just the way we are, and we can even make it a heavier dose, and it's knocking out everything they have. Or there's a smarter strategy that you make a deal."

But he added: "We're locked and loaded. We're ready to go."

Growing concern over new threats to shipping in the Red Sea from Yemen's Houthis helped push the price of crude oil back over $100 (£74.96) a barrel this week - the highest level since May.

But it dropped again on Friday afternoon, with Brent futures down more than US$4 (£3.00) to a little over $96 (£72.07), according to the Reuters news agency, which reported the fall occurred after the successful passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait by two Chinese-chartered supertankers.

Following the exchange of fire early on Saturday, the Houthis' Ansarollah media posted on Telegram, "The Saudi enemy's targeting of civilian facilities in Hodeida and Kamaran island constitutes a dangerous escalation," adding: "We affirm that these recent crimes will not go unanswered."

Saudi authorities did not immediately respond.

The US and UK are set to hold a conference in London next week to discuss the Strait of Hormuz, the BBC understands. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Dan Caine will attend the conference, which was first reported by Axios.

It comes as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is scheduled to meet the US president at the White House on Tuesday.

In June, the US and Iran agreed on a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to halt military operations and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, as well as to reach an agreement to end the war over the following 60 days.

But three weeks after it was signed, Trump declared the ceasefire "over" after Iranian attacks on ships in the strait, and US strikes in response.

title: ‘No time to waste’: Greece bids for Mount Olympus to be included on Unesco list of world heritage sites
excerpt:
Officials have long lobbied for peak that rises 2,918 metres above sea level to be given coveted designation

More than four decades have elapsed since Evangelos Geroliolios made his first ascent to t...
body_text:
Officials have long lobbied for peak that rises 2,918 metres above sea level to be given coveted designation

More than four decades have elapsed since Evangelos Geroliolios made his first ascent to the home of the ancient gods. At the top of Mount Olympus, on the rocky peak of Greece’s highest mountain, he felt unalloyed awe.

“I’ve never forgotten that unique moment, that unique feeling up there on the throne of Zeus,” recalled Geroliolios, who as mayor of Dion-Olympus now spends a great deal of his time administering the area around the site.

Described by Homer as the “seat of the immortals”, its craggy summit – where Zeus, the father of the gods, is said to have held court – rises 2,918 metres above the sea.

“You get this incredible sense of place, fused by myth, beauty and the weight of history – all of which we want to share and hope will be recognised internationally,” he said.

Greek officials have long lobbied for Mount Olympus to be included on the Unesco list of world heritage sites; soon champions of the cause will learn if the site will finally be granted the coveted designation.

The World Heritage Committee is scheduled to begin discussing the nomination on Sunday at its 48th session, now under way in Busan, South Korea. The annual meeting ends on 29 July.

Greece first proposed the mountain’s inclusion on the list of places considered by Unesco to be “of outstanding value to humanity” in 2014, citing both its cultural and environmental significance.

The area was declared as Greece’s first national forest in 1938, in tribute to the uniqueness of terrain covered not only by verdant forest but alpine fields, gorges, ravines and springs, all within close proximity of the sea.

Litochoro, the nearest town to the mountain, lies three miles (5km) away from breathtaking beaches practically at the foot of the mountain.

In recognition of its abundance of flora and fauna, Unesco designated Olympus a biosphere reserve in 1981. Further environmental protection came in the form of a presidential decree, when the mountain was declared a national park, in 2021.

“But,” says Geroliolios, “becoming a world heritage site would not only be important for Greeks. It would speak to the entire planet. Olympus is up there with the Parthenon and it’s vital that we safeguard this environment of myth and history. For us, protection is the alpha and omega.”

Last year, the committee inscribed 26 new properties on Unesco’s World Heritage list, bringing the total number of sites to 1,428 across 170 countries. Of the 21 in Greece, only two have been inducted as mixed cultural and natural world heritage sites.

Under an international treaty overseen by Unesco, the treasures, which include landmarks such as the Great Wall of China, the Egyptian Pyramids and the Taj Mahal, automatically become protected zones.

Increasingly the designation is regarded as a bulwark against the depredations of development and overtourism. Like much of Greece, the mountain’s popularity has soared over the past decade, with about 500,000 visitors recorded last year.

It is a number that is widely predicted to rise on the back of revived interest in the ancient world after the 17 July release of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey. The record-breaking blockbuster, inspired by Homer’s epic, was partially filmed in Greece, which also helped subsidise the movie.

“We’re happy to have tourists but more of them will mean more risks,” said Dimitris Pappas, the deputy director of the Olympus national park management agency.

“There’s no doubt that if the area is declared a Unesco world heritage site it will help contribute to the mountain’s protection. If we lose what we have it will be a catastrophe.”

Pappas said by far the biggest threat to the site was forest firesexacerbated by climate breakdown.

“They could be averted with extra funds to improve fire protection measures, including clearing walking paths and building shelters. River bridges and roads could be upgraded, too.”

World heritage sites are provided with technical support and financial assistance from Unesco, which also gives expert advice to help preserve the monuments.

Tourists visiting the site this week said the designation was not only deserved, but overdue. “It’s not just a good idea, it’s the best idea,” enthused Lenka Hotmarova, 62, from the Czech Republic. “There’s room for improvement along the trails and it would help raise awareness about the need for preservation. It should have happened earlier.”

Greece has also highlighted the mountain’s religious significance, citing the discovery of an open-air sanctuary, on one of the mountain’s lowest peaks, in its nomination file.

The sanctuary is believed to have been described by Plutarch, the philosopher historian, in the second century AD in connection with animal sacrifices made to Zeus.

Mount Olympus is thought to be home to the highest altitude chapel in the Christian Orthodox world with Byzantine monasteries and other places of worship built into its folds and peaks.

The bid’s outcome is still far from certain. Advisory bodies from the International Council on Monuments and Sites (ICOMOS) and International Union for Conservation of Nature are reported to have recommended further details with the draft agenda of the Unesco meeting in Busan suggesting the nomination will be referred back to Greece – prolonging the quest further.

At a time of soaring tourism, that worries Geroliolios. “It’s all about balance,” he says. “Olympus’s carrying capacity has reached its limit.”

Designation as a world heritage site would “place greater responsibility on our part to protect the environment”, he said, adding: “But even if we don’t succeed, there’s no time to waste. Further protective measures have to be taken.”

title: California trans suspect arrested in mother's killing after neighbor recalls heated argument
excerpt: Fox News' Bryan Llenas reports on the ongoing investigation into the murder of New Jersey mom Brooke Hanlon, found stabbed in her home. More than a month after the incident, no arrests have been made,...
body_text:
Fox News' Bryan Llenas reports on the ongoing investigation into the murder of New Jersey mom Brooke Hanlon, found stabbed in her home. More than a month after the incident, no arrests have been made, and authorities remain tight-lipped about key details, including the 911 call and the cooperation of her husband, James Connor Hanlon. Neighbors are baffled by the unsolved case in Chester, N.J.

A California man was arrested this week in connection with his mother's killing, authorities said.

Angela Caprioli, 61, was found dead Monday at a home in Laguna Beach, according to the Laguna Beach Police Department. The New York Post identified Caprioli and the suspect, Safford Wolfson, as mother and son.

Wolfson, 36, was arrested Thursday on suspicion of murder after investigators previously identified him as a person of interest in the case.

RETIRED MATH PROFESSOR CHARGED AFTER WIFE, AN AIRLINE METEOROLOGIST, FOUND SHOT DEAD: COPS

Angela Caprioli and Safford Wolfson. Wolfson was arrested on suspicion of murder after authorities said Caprioli was found dead at a Laguna Beach home. The New York Post identified the pair as mother and son. (Angela Caprioli via Facebook)

Police said officers responded to a home in the 1300 block of Dunning Drive shortly after 11 a.m. for a death investigation and found Caprioli deceased.

The circumstances surrounding her death remain under investigation.

Neighbor Dustin Pettit said he witnessed Wolfson and Caprioli engaged in what appeared to be a heated argument at the home days before the alleged killing.

FLORIDA MAN ARRESTED AFTER SUSPECTED HUMAN REMAINS FOUND BURIED AT PROPERTY WHERE HIS FATHER LIVED

Angela Caprioli, 61, was found dead at a Laguna Beach, California, home on July 20, authorities said. (Angela Caprioli via Facebook)

"I saw her outside talking with him and it seemed like a pretty hostile conversation," Pettit told The California Post.

"She turned around and went inside and slammed the door, like she was fed up with whatever was going on."

Pettit also told CBS Los Angeles that Wolfson had moved into the home about six months earlier.

"He was pretty mysterious. He wasn't talking to us, you know, he would come outside, smoke a cigarette and play some guitar," he said. "That's kinda the extent of the relationship we've had with him over the last six months or so."

Angela Caprioli was found dead at a Laguna Beach home. The New York Post identified Safford Wolfson, who was later arrested on suspicion of murder, as her son. (Angela Caprioli via Facebook)

According to the New York Post, social media accounts associated with Wolfson identify the account holder as transgender.

The outlet also reported that Wolfson wrote on Facebook in 2024: "Not even my mom wants to hang out with me man… talk about lame-o!"

Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: House Republicans confront NJ governor over 6,600 noncitizens registered to vote in alleged software failure
excerpt:
Democratic lawmakers say New Jersey's voter registration error demands accountability but reject claims it points to widespread election fraud. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Ninetee...
body_text:
Democratic lawmakers say New Jersey's voter registration error demands accountability but reject claims it points to widespread election fraud. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

Nineteen House Republicans are demanding answers from New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill on how approximately 6,600 self-identified noncitizens were registered to vote and cast 400 ballots in what the state described as a software failure.

The group put the question to Sherrill in a letter published on Friday afternoon.

"Despite those answers, a software failure reportedly transmitted their information for voter registration between June 2023 and June 2024. This was not a minor clerical discrepancy," the group wrote in the letter. "It was a catastrophic breakdown of the most basic safeguard in our election system: ensuring that only eligible American citizens are registered and permitted to vote. How do you know this was just a software glitch and not a nefarious act?"

The letter continues to underscore Republican-led concerns that lawmakers are inviting election security liabilities without passing legislation to shore up voter identification and implement federal standards to ensure proof of citizenship.

GOP ERUPTS OVER 6,600 NONCITIZEN VOTERS FOUND IN BLUE STATE AS SCANDAL DEEPENS: ‘WORSE THAN ANYONE EXPECTED’

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill pictured shortly after taking office in January. (Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/Getty Images)

Its signatories included Rep. Jefferson Van Drew, R-N.J., and Rep. Chris Smith, R-N.J., two of New Jersey’s three Republican congressmen.

Notably, the third, Rep. Tom Kean Jr., R-N.J., did not join.

The system failure originally came to the public’s attention when Sherrill disclosed the issue in an announcement on Tuesday.

"Last week I learned that a serious software error in New Jersey’s Motor Vehicle System led to the registration of roughly 6,600 people who indicated that they were not U.S. citizens between June 2023 and June 2024, almost three years prior to my taking office," Sherrill said.

NEW JERSEY REMOVES 6,600 PEOPLE FROM VOTER ROLLS WHO WERE ELIGIBLE TO CAST A BALLOT FOR 2024 ELECTION

then-New Jersey Democratic gubernatorial candidate, U.S. Rep. Mikie Sherrill, D-N.J. speaks to the media after casting her vote on November 4, 2025 in Montclair, New Jersey. (Eduardo Munoz Alvarez/Getty Images)

"These individuals answered ‘no’ when asked on a keypad whether they were a U.S. citizen when applying for drivers' licenses and identification cards, but through no fault of their own, the system registered them anyway."

Republicans in their letter listed a series of questions they said the state should answer, including what testing it normally conducts for voter roll maintenance, the specific counties where the improper ballots were cast, and whether Sherrill’s administration would support voter-ID legislation.

Rep. Mikie Sherrill casts her ballot at a polling location inside Hillside Elementary School in Montclair, N.J., on Nov. 4, 2025, during the New Jersey gubernatorial election. (John Lamparski/Bloomberg)

"Republicans have been sounding the alarm for years about weaknesses in voter-registration systems, inadequate voter-roll maintenance, and the danger that noncitizens may be registered and permitted to vote in national elections, which is illegal under federal law," the letter stated.

The group has requested a response to its questions no later than Aug. 21, 2026.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

U.S. Immigra...
body_text:
Department of Homeland Security officials confirmed an ICE detainer has been lodged against an illegal immigrant accused of fatally crashing into two young boys in South Carolina. (WHNS)

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) are seeking custody of a Mexican citizen who authorities say entered the United States illegally through Texas in 2021 under the Biden administration and killed a Nashville restaurant owner.

After pleading guilty and being sentenced Tuesday to decades behind bars, ICE lodged an immigration detainer against Ulises Raigoza-Martinez, requesting that Tennessee officials notify the agency before his release, so federal authorities can take him into custody for removal proceedings, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

The case stems from a June 19, 2024, encounter in the parking lot of the Nashville restaurant Smokin' Thighs, where investigators claim Raigoza-Martinez stopped to steal tools from owner Matt Carney's pickup truck.

'SLAP ON THE WRIST': ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCKER'S SENTENCE IGNITES OUTRAGE AFTER CRASH KILLED 3

Matt Carney, owner of the Nashville restaurant Smokin' Thighs, died on July 4, 2024, after authorities say he was struck by a vehicle while confronting a man accused of stealing tools from his pickup truck. (DHS)

When Carney, 42, walked outside to confront the thief, Raigoza-Martinez sped away, striking the restaurateur with his vehicle, authorities said. Carney landed on the hood before being thrown to the pavement when Raigoza-Martinez turned the vehicle.

Carney suffered critical injuries and died at a Nashville hospital on July 4, 2024.

Police arrested Raigoza-Martinez in South Nashville on July 18, 2024. Two years later, on July 22, 2026, he pleaded guilty to murder, theft over $10,000, tampering with evidence and theft over $2,500, before being sentenced to 20 years in prison.

EXCLUSIVE: DHS SEEKS CUSTODY OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER TRUMP DEPORTATION, BIDEN RELEASE

Ulises Raigoza-Martinez pleaded guilty to murder, theft over $10,000, tampering with evidence and theft over $2,500 in the death of Nashville restaurant owner Matt Carney. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison. (DHS)

DHS Assistant Secretary Lauren Bis said Raigoza-Martinez "should NEVER have been in our country to commit this heinous murder."

"We will work with our state and local partners in Tennessee to ensure that he is handed over to ICE custody once his sentence is complete, so that we can remove him from our country," Bis said.

FILE - ICE is seeking custody of the suspect after he serves his prison sentence for the killing. (Paul Weaver/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

If Tennessee officials honor the ICE detainer, federal immigration authorities will take custody of Raigoza-Martinez after he completes his prison sentence so he can be placed into removal proceedings and deported.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: Azzi Fudd wins WNBA 3-point contest, becomes first rookie champion
excerpt:
Minnesota Lynx star Kayla McBride says the WNBA texted her agent just before the event, and considered it an unofficial invite. (This video contains AI-assisted content)

Azzi Fudd put on a historic s...
body_text:
Minnesota Lynx star Kayla McBride says the WNBA texted her agent just before the event, and considered it an unofficial invite. (This video contains AI-assisted content)

Azzi Fudd put on a historic shooting display during her first WNBA All-Star weekend. The Dallas Wings guard won Friday night’s 3-point contest, becoming the first rookie in league history to win the event.

Fudd finished the first round with 30 points, 10 shy of the maximum possible score. Portland Fire star Bridget Carleton was eliminated after scoring 19 in the round. Fudd took 27 shots, missing just six of her attempts en route to winning the coveted title.

Fudd acknowledged she experienced some nerves Friday night. "You saw ‘only’ six shots, but I feel like that was a lot," Fudd said. "But honestly, I was really nervous. I was excited."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Azzi Fudd of the Dallas Wings poses with the trophy after winning the Kia WNBA Skills Challenge STARRY 3-Point Contest at AT&T WNBA All-Star 2026 at Wintrust Arena in Chicago, Illinois, on July 24, 2026. (Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images)

Fudd added: "It's fun to do because... and I don't want to sound cocky... but it's easy to me, just the set shot. Take the ball from the rack; it really is muscle memory. It's what I've been doing since I was young."

Fudd entered the All-Star break averaging 2.2 shots from beyond the 3-point arc this season. She's knocked down 53 total 3-pointers so far during her rookie year.

LIBERTY'S SABRINA IONESCU ADDRESSES ABSENCE FROM WNBA 3-POINT CONTEST: 'NEVER OFFICIALLY GOT INVITED'

While injuries impacted Fudd's college basketball career, Dallas valued her overall talent and took her with the first selection in April's WNBA Draft.

Azzi Fudd of the Dallas Wings shoots during the Kia WNBA Skills Challenge STARRY 3-Point Contest at the WNBA All-Star 2026 at Wintrust Arena in Chicago, Illinois, on July 24, 2026. (Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images)

Fudd also said her injury setbacks came with an unexpected benefit. The repetitive shooting she did during rehab helped sharpen her form and build the rhythm needed to knock down shots from the same spots in Friday’s 3-point contest.

"That was a lot of chair shooting, a lot of stationary shots, so you get really good at shooting off of a rack and being stationary and robotic and having to knock your shot down."

Dallas Wings guard Azzi Fudd (35) reacts during the Kia WNBA Skills Challenge STARRY 3-Point Contest at the AT&T WNBA All-Star 2026 at Wintrust Arena in Chicago, Illinois, on July 24, 2026. (Geoff Stellfox/Getty Images)

Before the 3-point contest, the WNBA debuted another All-Star event in Chicago — the Shooting Stars competition.

Replacing the past skills challenge, the Shooting Stars competition featured four three-person teams. Each roster included one former player designated as a legend, one current player and one rising young player. Team Washington defeated Team Seattle to win the inaugural event.

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X, and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

Chantz Martin is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump spares no one at WHCA dinner, taking aim at Dems, press and his own Cabinet
excerpt:
President Donald Trump praised the new White House ballroom and military facility during the WHCA Dinner.

President Donald Trump struck a more conciliatory tone Friday at the rescheduled White House ...
body_text:
President Donald Trump praised the new White House ballroom and military facility during the WHCA Dinner.

President Donald Trump struck a more conciliatory tone Friday at the rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner, scrapping the combative speech he had prepared before an assassination attempt upended the annual event in April. The rewrite emphasized unity and gratitude, though the president still couldn't resist slipping in a few familiar jabs at the press while insisting: "The show must go on."

Trump returned to the stage just months after gunfire abruptly ended the organization’s annual banquet. An armed suspect, Cole Allen, stormed the event in what authorities say was an attempt to assassinate the president.

"The speech that I had ready just a short while. Oh, that was going to be a doozy. I was so psyched. I was going to rip people. And I don't know, just something changed it — really for the better. But I just wouldn't want to do that," Trump said to a room full of journalists and government officials.

"But we'll do a little ripping, if you don't mind. But it is true. I said, how do we handle this is going to be a different kind of evening. And it is. And in many ways it's a more beautiful evening, actually," he added.

TRUMP HEADS BACK TO CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER MONTHS AFTER GUNFIRE FORCED EVACUATION

President Donald Trump speaks during the 2026 White House Correspondents' Association Dinner. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

Trump teed up his typical walk-out song — Lee Greenwood's "God Bless the U.S.A." — and quickly jumped into joking about seeking a third term before striking a more serious chord as he thanked the Secret Service for its work, not only during the attack at the original Correspondents' Dinner, but for protecting him every day.

He delivered a speech that went longer than expected, talking for an hour and four minutes.

"Just like my presidency, the second time is always better. It's always better, and the third time will be better yet. I'm only kidding," Trump said to some chuckles throughout the room.

The president said he could not deliver the same speech he had planned for the first dinner, "ripping" the press, but said "it was for the better" that he changed his remarks for the second time around.

COLE ALLEN INDICTED BY GRAND JURY ON FOUR CHARGES RELATED TO ALLEGED TRUMP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT

He made various jokes aimed at not just Democrats but his own cabinet members.

"I hope that everyone finally got to enjoy their entire very delicious beef tenderloins, very special beef. And I want you all to know that Bobby Kennedy, who's right here personally, ran over the cow and his car," said Trump.

White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt and US President Donald Trump attend the 2026 White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) Dinner at the Waldorf Astoria in Washington, DC. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

TRUMP HEADS BACK TO CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER MONTHS AFTER GUNFIRE FORCED EVACUATION

He took aim at California Governor Gavin Newsom, former vice president Kamala Harris, possible 2028 presidential candidate Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker among other Democratic lawmakers and candidates.

" You can't have somebody like a J.B. Pritzker who I understand is not president, sadly. But, you know, some people say never used a fat word. And I know I would never call anybody fat," said Trump.

"I have my own problems, you know, it's not like I'm perfect, sir. In the back. Don't call him a fat pig, okay? That's. I'm sticking up for him. Don't call him you. You can't do that, sir. You can't call J.B. Pritzker a fat pig," said Trump.

Trump mocked Chuck Schumer's criticism of Israel and his increasingly vocal positions on the Israel-Hamas war.

"I'm going to send him a beautiful Palestinian outfit tomorrow so he can greet Bibi Netanyahu when he comes to town next week," joked Trump.

He used the moment to call for term limits, saying, "all joking aside, I do think we need term limits in Congress."

"The other day, a senator I knew got a text... 'When you get home, I want to have you immediately come up the stairs and make love to me.' And he said, 'I can't do both," joked Trump, saying that he can't both walk upstairs and have sex—he only has enough energy for one of those activities.

US President Donald Trump wears a "Trump 2028" hat while he speaks during the 2026 White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) Dinner. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

The WHCA honored U.S. Secret Service Officer Victor Gonzales during Friday's dinner in recognition of his actions in helping stop Allen from entering the ballroom.

The computer scientist from Torrance, California, traveled from Los Angeles to Washington, D.C. by Amtrak after purchasing a one-way ticket. Court filings say he sent a manifesto to family and friends shortly before the attack, describing political motivations and apologizing for his actions.

Allen has pleaded not guilty to charges including attempting to assassinate the president, discharging a firearm during a crime of violence, transporting a firearm across state lines and assaulting a federal officer with a deadly weapon.

"The attempted mass murder at the Washington Hilton, that's what it could have been, was an assault on our democracy itself," Trump said in his speech, which spanned from jabs at Democrats, the press and some jokes at the expense of his own Cabinet.

PHOTO OF TRUMP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT SUSPECT COLE ALLEN IN HOTEL ROOM RELEASED AS DOJ SEEKS TO KEEP HIM JAILED

Israeli-US magician Oz "Oz the Mentalist" Pearlman performs during the 2026 White House Correspondents' Association Dinner.  (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

"One officer placed himself directly in harm's way and engaged the armed suspect, even after gunfire struck his protective vest. He stayed in the fight and the attacker was stopped," said Weijia Jiang, former WHCA president presenting the award to Gonzales.

"I know many of us have wondered. What if he hadn't acted in that exact way? What if he had waited a few more seconds? His courage that night reflects the core values of Secret Service duty, justice, courage, honesty and loyalty, and as a commitment to safeguarding his country and community," said Jiang.

During the speech, Trump highlighted his White House Ballroom following heat for the $200 million project, pointing to the lawsuits.

FIRST ON FOX: WHITE HOUSE REVEALS WHO’S JOINING TRUMP AT CORRESPONDENTS’ DINNER — AND WHO CAN’T ATTEND

"In light of what we went through, I think, people understand it. It's going to be amazing, a phenomenal one of the biggest drone ports anywhere in the world," Trump said, referencing gunfire at the first WHCA Dinner.

Trump said that he "predicts" the WHCA would use the space for future dinners.

Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. arrives for the White House Correspondents' Association (WHCA) Dinner,. (REUTERS/Jonathan Ernst)

He also vowed to attemd next year’s WHCA dinner.

"They said, 'Would you do it next year?' I said, 'I will be back next year,'" Trump said. "Now, if you get really, really nasty, maybe not. I don't know. But we're going to be back next year."

In his closing remarks, Trump said he has a "scoop" for the press announcing he is running for the fourth time.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

title: ‘The show must go on’: Trump returns to rescheduled White House press gala
excerpt:
United States President Donald Trump returned to the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, three months after a gunman upended the event.

“As I said three months ago, the show must go on,” ...
body_text:
United States President Donald Trump returned to the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, three months after a gunman upended the event.

“As I said three months ago, the show must go on,” Trump said at the start of his speech on Friday, after a lengthy awards ceremony, during which several journalists, including CNN’s Wolf Blitzer, spoke.

The annual – and perennially controversial – event had originally been held in April, but it was swiftly derailed after a gunman attempted to storm the proceedings in an alleged effort to assassinate Trump.

“Just like my presidency, the second time is always better and the third time will be better yet,” Trump quipped, before raising his hands at the crowd and saying, “I’m only kidding.”

The US president is limited to two terms by the Constitution, but Trump has been facetiously floating the idea of running for a third time.

The rescheduled dinner took place in the ballroom of the Waldorf Astoria hotel, with a guest list of 700 people, much smaller compared with April’s botched gathering.

“It was an assault on our democracy itself; it was a very serious situation,” Trump said of the alleged assassination attempt.

He lauded some of his aides, including Pete Hegseth, Steve Miller and Tom Holman, for showing “bravery” during the incident.

“They were standing on tables, when most of you were under the tables,” he said.

Alleged gunman Cole Tomas Allen had stormed a security gate at the gala venue, the Washington Hilton, armed with guns and knives. He was accused by prosecutors of shooting and injuring a Secret Service officer before he was stopped.

Allen is facing federal charges of attempting to assassinate the president.

“Many people yelled, ‘Get down. Get down,’ which caused Nicki Minaj to start twerking,” Trump said on Friday.

As journalists in attendance forced a muted laugh, Trump added: “She’s the only one who knew what that meant.”

Trump later used the event to rebuke political opponents, presenting his attacks as jokes. He called Democratic California Governor Gavin Newsom “newscum”, questioned Congresswoman Ilhan Omar’s intelligence, and pretended that someone in the audience was calling Illinois Governor JB Pritzker a “fat pig” to appear that he was not uttering the insult himself.

The US president also called top Democratic Senator Chuck Schumer “Palestinian” as an insult.

Earlier in the evening, Trump entered the ballroom to polite applause.

“This is the largest gathering of people with Trump derangement syndrome,” he said, referring to journalists.

The US president has had a historically caustic relationship with the dinner, but this year, he touted the celebration this year, calling it a “very good thing” and a “HOT ticket”.

White House Correspondents’ Association president Weijia Jiang of CBS News, which was acquired by pro-Israel investor David Ellison last year, thanked Trump for his support, and for showing up for the second time in three months.

“Tonight our message is this: We are back,” she said. “We will not be intimidated. We refuse to let an act of violence have the final word.”

Trump’s enthused attendance represented a sea change from his first term, beginning in 2017, when the newly elected president declared the soiree “dead” and declined to attend over the next four years.

Beyond Trump, the White House Correspondents’ Dinner has long been a lightning rod for criticism among media professionals, with some journalists arguing that reporters should not be chummy with the politicians they cover. Calls for the dinner to be abandoned entirely only grew after the April incident.

body_text:
President Donald Trump could not help but poke fun at the New York Mets for losing "all the time" despite their sky-high payroll this season.

The New York Mets have been dealt yet another blow on the injury front, this time with star Juan Soto exiting the game.

The Mets hosted the defending World Champion Los Angeles Dodgers — fresh off a White House visit — on Friday evening.

It was an eventful evening at the ballpark, as actress Emma Stone was there filming a movie and took some time to chat with Soto before the game.

TRUMP CAN'T HELP BUT TAKE JAB AT METS IN SPEECH WHILE PRAISING BRAVES CEO: 'THEY LOSE ALL THE TIME'

However, that may have been the highlight of the night for Soto.

The 27-year-old drew two walks, but partway through the sixth inning, the Mets took Soto out of the game.

The calf injury has been lingering for a while and has been on the Mets' radar. In fact, it first surfaced on July 16. Soto was even given time off earlier this week to address it.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Mets star Juan Soto left Friday's game against the Los Angeles Dodgers with left calf soreness. ((Photo by Mary DeCicco/MLB Photos via Getty Images))

Before the game, interim manager Andy Green even addressed it.

"It’s improving for him," Green said, per MLB.com. "Hopefully after today, we don’t have to talk about it anymore."

Unfortunately, they will, and on social media, Mets fans were trying to handle the latest bit of injury news.

Soto was the only All-Star for the Mets this season, which underscores what a problem it is if he's not in the lineup.

Juan Soto of the New York Mets walks back to the dugout after striking out in the first inning against the Cincinnati Reds at Great American Ball Park in Cincinnati, Ohio, on June 16, 2026. (Dylan Buell/Getty Images)

Through 84 games this season, Soto is batting .283 with 83 hits and 21 home runs. He is in the second year of a 15-year, $765 million deal that he signed with the Mets in December 2024.
