The organization is resilient and will be able to replace those killed."

A former senior Department of War official told Fox News Digital the U.S. has at its disposal cruise missiles and long-range bombers. Attack drones would probably not come into play, and the U.S. Naval Institute’s Fleet Tracker shows no American aircraft carriers anywhere near African waters, effectively ruling out carrier operations.

However, Ekman believes airstrikes are under consideration, noting "JNIM and ISIS are a threat to U.S. interests, and are ascendant in West Africa."

Paul Tilsley is a veteran correspondent who has reported from four continents for more than three decades. Based in Johannesburg, South Africa, he can be followed on X @paultilsley.

title: Australian households face prospect of interest rate hike and petrol prices rising above $2 a litre
excerpt:
Economists’ warning comes as escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude oil back above $US100 a barrel

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian households face t...
body_text:
Economists’ warning comes as escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude oil back above $US100 a barrel

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australian households face the prospect of a Reserve Bank interest rate hike and petrol prices above $2 a litre over the coming weeks, economists warn, as the escalating Middle East crisis pushes global crude back above $US100 a barrel.

Financial markets now see an even chance the RBA board will deliver a fourth cash rate increase at the next meeting on 11 August.

Warwick McKibbin, the director of the ANU’s Centre for Applied Macroeconomic Analysis, said crude oil prices were likely to stay elevated for “at least a year” as the US-Iran war entered a new and more dangerous phase.

The Houthis’ blockade of Saudi Arabian oil through the Red Sea and the Ukrainians’ increasingly successful destruction of Russian energy infrastructure had heaped further pressure on global oil supply, McKibbin said.

“Getting access to supplies looks different now than it did a few months ago. All the reserves have been run down, particularly in the US. It’s quite a serious situation for the world to be in.”

The phasing down of the government’s fuel tax relief to 16 cents per litre and this month’s 37% jump in the international Brent crude benchmark has pushed the cost of unleaded to $1.80 a litre, up from a recent low of about $1.50 at the beginning of the month, according to Motormouth.

Johnathan McMenamin, a senior economist at Barrenjoey, said higher global prices and the end of the remaining fuel excise discount after 2 August meant unleaded would march back above $2 a litre over coming weeks.

“That is an uncomfortable level for households, but it isn’t something we are too unfamiliar with,” McMenamin said.

Diesel prices are up by about 50 cents in July to about $2.20 a litre in the major East Coast cities.

Climbing fuel prices will be another blow to the Reserve Bank’s efforts to bring inflation down while managing the damage to the economy from high energy costs.

McMenamin believes the central bank will pull the trigger next month – a view he had even before the latest developments in the Middle East.

“People will start to see fuel prices go up again, and the concern will be that inflation expectations will once again lift among households and businesses,” he said.

“It does matter for how long the oil price is $US100 a barrel – if it’s here for only a couple of days and quickly reverses, then that will provide some relief.

“But, clearly, we’ve all lost confidence in where it [the oil price] will be in six months.”

With the economy already slowing sharply, not all economists are convinced that the RBA needs to hike again.

Sally Auld, NAB’s chief economist, said she had never assumed the sharp drop in oil prices during the ceasefire was sustainable, even without a major escalation in the conflict.

“But we did think it was going to be just one big spike around March and April, before it settled down. Now it looks like it will be more of a grind, or maybe rolling mini-spikes,” Auld said.

Inflation remains too high but is tracking a little below where the RBA had forecast, Auld said, while unemployment was running a little higher. That combination would be enough to keep the RBA on hold while they waited for a slowing economy to take the steam out of price pressures, she said.

Auld warned that not all Australians will be able to cope with higher borrowing costs and climbing fuel costs.

“If you get an intensification of cost of living pressures plus another rate hike, for a certain segment of households that would be a pretty challenging situation and you would start to worry the economic adjustment won’t be so benign.”

title: Pauline Hanson’s domestic violence comments were no stumble
excerpt:
The One Nation leader has allied herself with men’s rights activists for years, consistently suggesting women routinely make false allegations of violence

Follow our Australia news live blog for late...
body_text:
The One Nation leader has allied herself with men’s rights activists for years, consistently suggesting women routinely make false allegations of violence

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

For a decade, Pauline Hanson has been beating the same drum.

Her comments this week – suggesting domestic violence was a “two-way street” and questioning why women did not simply leave abusive relationships – have caused significant concern and been labelled “dangerous” by experts and other commentators.

But they are not, as they’ve been portrayed, another “gaffe” by the stumbling One Nation leader as she attempts to stabilise her party’s polls that show it might become a new electoral force in Australia.

The comments make plain something that has been a driving force for the populist leader since her return to parliament in 2016.

One Nation’s political ascendancy in recent months has been built on replicating anti-immigrant and hard right pivots in the United States and the UK. Hanson’s own second coming was built on an allyship with groups of anti-feminist men and heavily influenced by domestic violence allegations against her son, Adam Hanson, which she says were false.

In 2019, Hanson used parliamentary privilege to call her former daughter-in-law “nasty” and accuse her of making false claims about her son. She has consistently – inside and outside parliament – made claims, rejected by experts and evidence, that suggest women routinely make false allegations of violence for advantage in the family law system.

Speaking in 2017, on domestic violence orders, Hanson said: “Women, mostly women, are going around throwing them around left, right and centre.”

In 2021 on Sky News, Hanson said: “There are men who have been accused of these things that didn’t, it didn’t happen.

“It shows you how lies and perjury are leading to the failure of Australia’s family law system and contributing to the death of 21 men by suicide and the murder of one woman each week.”

The “21 men” figure has been repeatedly cited by Hanson, her colleague Malcolm Roberts, and others in One Nation as a campaigning point. The figure comes from a men’s rights organisation, the Australian Brotherhood of Fathers (ABF), and has been debunked by factcheckers.

The ABF have been among Hanson’s biggest cheerleaders since her re-election. Roberts has been particularly close to the group, visiting several times, and recording a special video message for a gathering.

One of the first things Roberts did after a federal parliament hearing in 2019 – when he claimed without evidence there were “many instances” of women making up domestic violence allegations – was to phone the ABF’s founder, Leith Erikson.

The ABF has claimed in Facebook posts to have received donations from One Nation, and the political party has held community barbecues in support of the men’s group.

The trope that women fabricate violence claims against men is a common grievance of men’s rights groups, but experts say there is no evidence to support this.

After the 2019 election, Hanson’s return to the senate became more than a political curiosity. The Morrison government, four seats short of a senate majority, suddenly needed her support to pass legislation.

The government’s sop to Hanson was to accede to her request for a family law inquiry, and to make her the deputy chair (she introduced herself at hearings as the “co-chair”). 
 It is particularly instructive, for all those playing along at home and wondering what One Nation might do with newfound political influence, to understand that the last time Hanson was in a position to ask for something, she chose an inquiry that became a formal platform for misogynists and groups pushing unsupported claims that the system is loaded against men.

Hanson livestreamed the hearings to her Facebook page. Commenters called expert witnesses and MPs things like “man-hater” and “dirty snake”.

The hearings in March 2020 took place less than a month after the murders of Hannah Clarke and her children.

When an expert witness, the Griffith University law professor Zoe Rathus, mentioned the case, Hanson responded:

“I totally agree that what happened to Hannah and her children was horrendous and should never happen. But it’s on both sides. I have read your report, and it’s all about women. Do you agree that there are men who are aggrieved, men who face domestic violence, men who are taking their own lives?

“Do you admit that there are men facing domestic violence?”
 Rathus responded: “I would prefer if you didn’t ask me whether I ‘admit’ things. I’m not really here to admit things. I’m here to present my research.

“The statistics are very clear that domestic violence is something that is very gendered and that violence in the home happens more often by men towards women.”

Her comments this week, in the shadow of four more alleged domestic violence homicides, have understandably triggered more backlash because of One Nation’s political ascendancy.

As a fringe politician needing only to win a senate quota every six years, Hanson’s views only needed to appeal to a small, angry cohort.

The common wisdom is that as One Nation heads for the mainstream – its founder will need to temper her more extreme ideas to keep her coalition of disengaged and aggrieved voters together.

Ben Smee is Guardian Australia’s Queensland state correspondent

title: Middle East crisis latest: US carries out strikes across Iran as Tehran targets American bases in region
excerpt:
Latest attacks come after Trump vowed ‘major military punishment’ for Tehran and its Houthi allies

Benjamin Netanyahu will meet Donald Trump at the White House on Tuesday, the Israeli prime minister’...
body_text:
Latest attacks come after Trump vowed ‘major military punishment’ for Tehran and its Houthi allies

Benjamin Netanyahu will meet Donald Trump at the White House on Tuesday, the Israeli prime minister’s office said.

“As part of the visit, the prime minister will meet with President Trump at the White House on Tuesday and attend the funeral service for Senator Lindsey Graham, a friend of Israel,” Netanyahu’s office said, adding that he will depart for Washington on Monday.

Netanyahu’s visit comes at a time when tensions have mounted between the two leaders over the handling of the war with Iran and as Trump threatens to escalate US military action.

Since Trump’s return to the White House last year, the two have already met six times, but this will be the first such meeting in five months. At the last one in February, Netanyahu made the case for the joint offensive against Iran that Trump launched with him weeks later.

Iran has pushed back on a New York Times (paywall) report from Thursday that Tehran had rejected a US ceasefire deal presented by the Iraqi prime minister, calling the report “completely diversionary and misleading,” according to state media IRNA.

The NYT reported that the proposal was the only one on the table, and Tehran was not interested in a temporary deal which left the question of control of the strait of Hormuz unresolved, citing Iranian officials.

The IRNA report claimed the proposal was for a “temporary 10-day ceasefire”. Full details of the proposal have not been published.

“Iran has always regarded diplomacy as having intrinsic value,” an unnamed Iranian official said, according to IRNA. “The problem of the escalation of conflict in the region stems exclusively from the United States’ breach of its promises and violation of the commitments contained in the June 18 memorandum of understanding.”

Baghdad has also denied the NYT report. Ali al-Zaidi’s trip to Iran followed his recent visit to the White House where he met with Donald Trump.

The Iraqi prime minister’s media office said the “claims” in the report were “completely baseless and had no connection to reality”, according to a statement published by the Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The office urged media outlets “to verify information, rely on official sources and refrain from circulating unsubstantiated reports or claims attributed to anonymous sources”.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps warned civilians in the Middle East on Friday to stay away from US forces, state media reported.

In an interview carried out by state TV, the IRGC said:

double quotation markWe warn the general public in countries where American soldiers are stationed to immediately stay out of a radius of 500 metres from the places where American soldiers are hiding, in order to be safe.

Jordan’s military said it intercepted seven missiles and six drones launched by Iran on Friday.

The military said the interceptions, performed by air defence systems and air force planes, “resulted in no casualties or material damage,” according to AFP.

Earlier on Friday, the Iranian army said it had launched drone attacks targeting US military personnel and military targets in Bahrain and Jordan after the US carried out its 13th consecutive night of strikes against Iran.

US missiles struck targets across Iran on Friday after Donald Trump vowed “major military punishment” for Tehran and its Houthi allies in Yemen for extending the Middle East war to a second major shipping chokepoint, the mouth of the ⁠Red Sea.

The US Central Command said it targeted Iranian military command centres, communication networks, drone storage facilities, coastal surveillance sites and maritime capabilities.

Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported that explosions were reported in Khondab, Khorramabad, Konarak and Jask.

Meanwhile, as Reuters reports, ​Iranian armed forces responded by firing a wave of retaliatory attacks on at US bases in neighbouring Arab countries and warning people there that they may strike non-military buildings used by US personnel.

The Iranian army said it used drones to target facilities in Bahrain and Jordan, with attacks also reported in Kuwait and Iraq.

It said Trump’s threats only strengthened its resolve.

title: How dangerous are wildfires and how can we stop them from getting worse?
excerpt:
The conditions for ferocious fires are expected to worsen as the planet heats up, putting more people at risk

Fierce wildfires after back-to-back heatwaves have forced tens of thousands of people acr...
body_text:
The conditions for ferocious fires are expected to worsen as the planet heats up, putting more people at risk

Fierce wildfires after back-to-back heatwaves have forced tens of thousands of people across southern Europe to flee their homes, while powerful infernos across Canada and the US choke big cities with thick smoke.

Wildfires directly kill hundreds of people each year. Though they may seem apocalyptic, the death toll is far lower than from floods, which kill thousands, and from heatwaves, which kill hundreds of thousands.

But when you factor in smoke, the human cost rises rapidly. The latest study estimates that the air pollution spewed by wildfires kills a staggering 1.5 million people each year. The toxic fumes can reach so far that tendrils of smoke from Australian bushfires have menaced South America, while smoke from Canadian fires – which regularly suffocate cities across the US – have fouled the air in Europe. Last year, a study attributed 22,000 early deaths in Europe to Canadian wildfire smoke in 2023, out of a total of 82,000 deaths.

Many things can spark a wildfire: natural causes such as lightning, faulty infrastructure such as downed power lines, or people behaving badly. Devastating blazes in recent years have been started by smokers tossing cigarette butts, tourists failing to put out campfires, and even arsonists intentionally setting nature alight.

But whether those sparks turn into small fires or raging blazes depends on the weather. Fires need hot, dry fuel to burn, and they spread further with strong winds.

Fossil fuel pollution has heated the planet by about 1.3C, raising the risk of prolonged heat that turns forests and grasslands into tinderboxes. In some regions, such as the Mediterranean, global heating is also fuelling droughts that dry out lush greenery.

Scientists have found that such shifts have made the wildfires that have happened this year in places including California, South Korea and Australia more likely – in some cases doubling the chance of extreme weather conditions that help fires spread.

Even as the planet has heated up, the area torched by fires has fallen. This is because people have taken nature that used to burn freely and turned it into farms or cities – in recent decades mainly in Africa – that stop the spread of flames. The latest models find land use changes and other human drivers have shrunk the burned area by 19.1% since 1900, while climate changes increased it by 15.8% – resulting in a small decline of 3.3% overall.

The conditions for ferocious fires are expected to worsen as the planet bakes. Two separate indices of fire weather project a steady rise in the number of days with high fire danger as temperatures inch higher, a recent study found.

By the end of the century, the total burned area is projected to rise by 40% even in an optimistic scenario for cutting carbon pollution, according to a separate study. In a worst-case scenario, it is set to double.

The danger that wildfires pose to people and property can drop sharply by managing land better. This can include creating fire breaks to stem the spread of an inferno, stopping new settlement in places prone to fires, and even sending herds of goats into abandoned farmland to graze away overgrown vegetation.

In some places firefighters are trying the technique of intentionally burning land to avoid a buildup of fuel that could lead to catastrophic fires – a long-running Indigenous practice in Australia and North America that European fire experts are starting to adopt.

Not on its own. Land abandonment and fire suppression is a big contributor to the buildup of fuel that allows blazes in parts of the US and the Mediterranean to explode into mega-fires, but in Canada, most of the burning takes place in boreal forests that were never managed by humans. These fires are being intensified by rising global average temperatures that worsen the risk of severe fire weather.

If you live somewhere at risk of wildfires, put a plan together before disaster strikes. This could include identifying safe routes and nearby shelters, and packing an emergency bag. Some fire services recommend creating a safe zone around your home that is free from leaves and flammable materials.

Experts say you should vacate immediately if authorities tell you to – or if your home is at risk but warnings have not come. To avoid the smoke, keep windows closed and use respirator masks.

title: Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed in West Bank shooting
excerpt:
It was the deadliest incident of its kind in the West Bank for months

At least four Palestinians and two Israelis have been killed in a shooting in the occupied West Bank - the deadliest single incid...
body_text:
It was the deadliest incident of its kind in the West Bank for months

At least four Palestinians and two Israelis have been killed in a shooting in the occupied West Bank - the deadliest single incident there in months.

There are conflicting accounts of the sequence of events in the northern village of Tal. Palestinians told the BBC that residents confronted Jewish settlers who were attacking them. An eyewitness said soldiers then arrived and started shooting.

Israel's military said it had responded to reports that hikers had been attacked. It said "terrorists stole the weapon" of a security guard and killed him.

It later said a soldier had also been killed, but did not give details. The IDF has not explained who killed the other Palestinians.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) says it is preparing for a major operation in the area and has cancelled soldiers' leave.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

Ahmed Zeidan, an eyewitness, told the BBC the latest incident began early in the morning, when locals in Tal rushed to confront about 30 settlers who were attacking Palestinian homes.

He said hand-to-hand clashes broke out in the presence of Israeli soldiers.

A local leader of the ruling Fatah party, Essam Saifi, told Reuters news agency that settlers opened fire before Israeli forces arrived and also started shooting.

He said two brothers and two of their cousins were among those killed. Palestinian officials said several other Palestinians were wounded.

The IDF said Palestinians began the attack.

It said soldiers had gone to Tal following a report of an attack on Israeli civilians who were hiking in the area. A security guard from a nearby settler outpost had gone to the scene and had his gun snatched by a Palestinian who used it against the Israelis, killing him.

Soldiers then "eliminated the terrorist who executed the terror attack", the IDF added.

It later said a 27-year-old soldier "fell during operational activity in the area of ​​the village". The circumstances of his death remain unclear.

The Israeli ambulance service said two Israelis were also wounded.

The Palestinian foreign ministry said it "condemns in the strongest terms the massacre" in Tal.

It said "the escalation of settler terrorism is a direct consequence of the protection, political backing, and complete impunity granted by the Israeli government and occupation forces".

"Official Israeli incitement continues to fuel and encourage these crimes, creating an environment in which settler violence flourishes without accountability," it added.

An AFP reporter at the site, south-west of Nablus, said roadblocks had been set up and troops were searching for additional suspects.

Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to act "with full force against the terrorists and those who orchestrate and sponsor them".

He called an emergency meeting with security officials, and reinforcements have been sent to the area, close to the settlement of Havat Gilad.

Since October 2023, 1,114 Palestinians have been killed there, the vast majority by the IDF, the UN says. It says at least 35 of the deaths have involved attacks by settlers.

The UN says 41 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. The settlements are illegal under international law.

title: Purported Nancy Guthrie note includes unusual demand that breaks basic ransom rule: retired FBI negotiator
excerpt:
New excerpts from a purported Nancy Guthrie ransom note appear inconsistent with the kidnapping-for-ransom motive, according to retired FBI negotiator and supervisory agent Jason Pack.

The latest rev...
body_text:
New excerpts from a purported Nancy Guthrie ransom note appear inconsistent with the kidnapping-for-ransom motive, according to retired FBI negotiator and supervisory agent Jason Pack.

The latest revelations about the purported first ransom note in the Nancy Guthrie case appear inconsistent with a kidnapping for ransom, according to a retired FBI negotiator.

"The fact that they wanted to cut off communication quickly suggests that they may not have had kidnapping for ransom as a primary motive, even though that's what this says," said Jason Pack, a retired FBI supervisory agent. "It doesn't seem like how a usual kidnapping goes down."

He said typical kidnappers want to keep communication channels open to negotiate payment and maintain leverage over the victim's family, making the reported demand for no further contact highly unusual.

NEW DETAILS FROM NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM DEMAND REVEALED, 'HER LIFE IS IN YOUR HANDS': REPORT

Savannah Guthrie will return to "Today" on Monday after a two-month absence since her mother, Nancy, went missing on Feb. 1. (Getty Images/Fox News Digital)

"The most telling sign is this no negotiation, no further contact line," Pack told Fox News Digital. "Genuine kidnappers wanna keep the line of communication open."

The sender did, however, incorporate known pressure tactics, including setting a deadline, making threats and telling the family that Guthrie knew what would happen if they failed to comply, Pack said.

But cutting off communication before the deadlines passed was also unusual, he added.

NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTE CLAIMED THAT SHE HAD DIED, BEEN ‘BURIED WITH NATURE,’ SOURCE SAYS

Annie Guthrie, her husband Tommaso Cioni, and Savannah Guthrie at their missing mother Nancy Guthrie's home on Monday, March 2, in Tucson, Arizona. (Fox News)

Guthrie was taken from her home in Tucson's Catalina Foothills neighborhood in the early morning hours of Feb. 1, according to the Pima County Sheriff's Department and the FBI. She has not been seen since, and no proof of life was ever provided.

In a second purported ransom note, the sender indicated Guthrie had died soon after she was taken and been buried "with nature."

New excerpts from what is reportedly the first note received by local media shed light on why Pack believes the communication departed from a traditional ransom demand.

NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTES DON'T MATCH SUSPECT'S BEHAVIOR, PROFILER SAYS: 'I DON'T BELIEVE THEY'RE REAL'

These two images were released by the FBI, recovered from Nancy Guthrie's Nest doorbell camera. It's unclear whether they show the same person. (FBI)

Briana Whitney, who was working for the Phoenix-based AZ Family news outlet when the case broke, joined "Crime Junkie" host Ashley Flowers on Wednesday to discuss the note her former outlet received. "Crime Junkie" declined to share copies of the text.

"Hello Savannah, we have your mother Nancy," she began, reading from what she said was the first note sent to local media. "She is safe but scared. She will be held for ransom, and once payment is received, she will be released unharmed. We will be holding her for a maximum of seven days."

As previously conveyed by authorities, the sender gave two deadlines with increased money demands the longer it took.

"Once payment is received to the Bitcoin address below, she will be released within 12 hours of deposit to a safe drop-off location back in Tucson," Whitney read. "If the payment is not received by the last deadline on Monday the 9th at 5 p.m., she will be killed. Your mother is aware of this, and her life is in your hands."

Deputies examine a flyer taped to Nancy Guthrie's mailbox on Sunday, Feb. 22, 2026. They were called to the scene after volunteer searchers and several streamers walked onto Guthrie's property with a shovel. (Michael Ruiz/Fox News Digital)

The sender left no room for further dialogue.

"It is in the best interest of everyone to have this completed as soon as possible," the note reportedly continued. "You will not be able to contact me from here on out. There will be no negotiation. Do not play games. Law enforcement will not be able to help you."

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

The note also included details that may have only been available to investigators and the suspect at the time, including the location of Guthrie's Apple Watch and details about the smashed floodlight in her backyard — but even that is not enough to pin down kidnapping for ransom as a motive, Pack said.

Savannah Guthrie poses alongside her mother Nancy Guthrie during a production break whilst hosting NBC's "Today Show" live from Australia. (Photo by Don Arnold/WireImage)

"The details about the security camera and the spotlight that was out, that proves that they know what the home was like, what the environment may have been like, but it's not a real proof of life," he said.

In most ransom kidnappings, he said, the abductors will want to prove they have possession of the victim and that the victim is alive.

"All these things put together don't seem really like they go with the kidnapping for ransom," he said.

Investigators appear to be split on the notes' authenticity. While one person has already pleaded guilty to sending an imposter ransom note to Guthrie's other daughter, Annie, and her husband Tommaso Cioni, that case is not believed to be connected to the notes sent to local media stations.

A well-wisher signs a banner that reads "Bring her home" and shows a photo of Nancy Guthrie, U.S. television journalist Savannah Guthrie's abducted elderly mother, at the KVOA newsroom, where Savannah worked earlier in her career, in Tucson, Arizona, U.S., Feb. 12, 2026. (Rebecca Noble/Reuters)

"The FBI and its task force partners have received several ransom notes over the course of this investigation," the FBI's Phoenix office said in a statement in June. "Some have been deemed to be extortion attempts without legitimacy. Other ransom demands may potentially be legitimate and are still being investigated as such. This case continues to be investigated as a kidnapping for ransom case. The FBI has and will continue to offer all assistance possible in the investigation — however local authorities remain the lead."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Some investigators said they were confident that the ransom demands are all bogus, while others are cautious about reaching that conclusion while Guthrie's whereabouts remain unknown, federal law enforcement sources told Fox News and Fox News Digital. Still, the two notes that Whitney mentioned have been deemed potentially authentic by investigators and by the Guthrie family.

The only known suspect remains publicly unidentified — a masked intruder who appeared on Nest doorbell camera video that the FBI recovered with help from Google.

He is described as standing between 5 feet, 9 inches and 5 feet, 10 inches tall with an average build. He was wearing a black Ozark Trail backpack. It remains unclear whether he acted alone.

The sum of rewards in the case is over $1.2 million.

Anyone with information is asked to dial 1-800-CALL-FBI. Tips can also be submitted anonymously to Tucson's Crime Stoppers affiliate at 520-88-CRIME.

title: Confusing product recall adds to US cyclospora outbreak uncertainty
excerpt:
Explosive diarrhea infection detected in 41 states with at least 72 sickened by new, as yet unknown source of parasite

Confusion abounds in the cyclospora outbreak that has sickened thousands in at l...
body_text:
Explosive diarrhea infection detected in 41 states with at least 72 sickened by new, as yet unknown source of parasite

Confusion abounds in the cyclospora outbreak that has sickened thousands in at least 41 states, as officials identify a new cluster of cases and more potential products come under scrutiny.

The recall of products during this outbreak of explosive diarrhea has been an unusual one, complicated by poor communication, politicization and the delay of a new regulatory rule could have helped trace the cyclosporiasis outbreak faster.

At least 72 people have been sickened by another as-yet unknown source of cyclospora, and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is now tracing back to the potential contamination source, according to an update from the agency on Wednesday.

It joins another investigation, still ongoing, that led to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms, a mega-producer based in the US with facilities in Mexico.

Officials in North Carolina also identified parsley and cilantro, in addition to lettuce, as potentially linked to the state’s 561 confirmed cases.

“The amount of cases we’re having right now is incredibly high, and it’s clear that there’s multiple outbreaks happening all at once,” said Katelyn Jetelina, science communicator and founder of Your Local Epidemiologist. “The news of another cluster isn’t too surprising to me. What is is how little information was given. The communication just continually is falling short, which is leaving all of us on the outside to put these puzzle pieces together.”

With all clusters of cases, “the key question is whether the source can stop,” said Joshua Sharfstein, a public health professor at Johns Hopkins University and former principal deputy commissioner at the FDA.

If there was a confined burst of contamination, the outbreak could end soon; but if the soil or water is still contaminated, “then there’s a risk of ongoing contamination, and that’s kind of what FDA has to worry about,” he said. And “the ability to say all the downstream products – that has traditionally been very hard”.

A new regulation was supposed to help with all of that.

Last year, the FDA proposed the Food Traceability Rule in order to more quickly track and identify foods at high risk of being contaminated by foodborne pathogens – including iceberg lettuce.

“This is exactly the sort of gap that the food traceability list is meant to close,” Jetelina said.

The new regulation was required by the Food Safety Modernization Act of 2011, and it was finally set to go into effect in January.

“Probably the most important thing about that law was that companies like Taylor Farms have to recognize the risk and have these processes to address it,” Sharfstein said.

But food suppliers asked for more time, and it is now planned to take effect in early 2028.

These epidemiological investigations are particularly important since cyclospora is so difficult to detect in produce. Without the updated rule, traceback investigations can take days or weeks – which can allow an outbreak to spread even more.

The recall from Taylor Farms has been plagued with confusion and reversals. Last Thursday, businesses supplied by Taylor Farms learned they should not use the lettuce before the FDA’s announcements, according to reporting by Consumer Reports. Executives also met with the White House and the FDA to distance themselves from the cyclospora outbreak, according to reporting by the New York Times and Bloomberg.

On Friday, the FDA warned against eating shredded iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell locations in Indiana, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and West Virginia – but the agency did not identify the producer at that point, noting only that they were located in Mexico.

Taylor Farms posted to Facebook on Friday afternoon that none of their salads or kits were associated with the outbreak, the Times also reported; the post appears to be deleted now, with no posts visible on their page since 8 July. The Taylor Farms website still said there were no active recalls. “In the rare event a product does not meet these standards, we take immediate action to remove affected items from distribution and notify our customers,” the website said.

The recall was posted later that evening, noting that the potentially contaminated lettuce had been shipped as recently as Thursday.

The voluntary recall said that 27 states might be affected by the contaminated lettuce. And it took the unusual approach of not listing brand names, instead using internal product numbers – which appear to correspond with products sold in stores such as Walmart and potentially restaurants such as Subway. That greatly complicated the ability of stores, restaurants and customers to know which products were involved in the recall.

“The actual recall notice from Taylor Farms was incredibly weird, because you had to decode it,” Jetelina said.

On Saturday, the FDA added an update: lettuce that was not part of the recall had tested positive for cyclospora. But on Sunday, the FDA deleted that line and said the test was a false positive. The recall still existed, FDA officials told journalists on Monday – despite confusing messaging from the supplier.

“Today, FDA apologized to us,” a statement on the Taylor Farms website read on Sunday, despite no public information about an apology. The farm added that “at this moment, FDA has not identified a single positive product test result for Cyclospora.” On Monday, the producer clarified that the recall was still in effect and that they were no longer sourcing iceberg lettuce from central Mexico for this growing season.

Cyclospora is notorious for being difficult to detect in produce; it’s much easier to find in the feces of humans, in whom the parasite thrives. It’s also possible for contamination of all sorts to be temporary in produce, which means investigators sometimes never have laboratory confirmation of which product or products spurred an outbreak. But there are other ways to identify contaminated products, like epidemiological investigations, Sharfstein said.

A spokesperson for Taylor Farms told the Guardian they were undertaking an independent investigation of its central Mexico facility, but did not answer questions about executives’ meeting with the White House and FDA, or provide clarity on when they first learned their product might be contaminated.

“When questions were raised about the source of the recent cyclospora outbreak, we immediately removed all potentially implicated product from the marketplace, and out of an abundance of caution we issued an even broader recall of all iceberg lettuce sourced from the region,” the spokesperson said.

US officials “remain focused on protecting the American people”, said Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services. The administration has “mounted a robust, science-based response to this cyclosporiasis outbreak, working closely with health departments in all 50 states, rapidly identifying known sources, and ensuring Americans have the information they need to protect themselves,” she added.

Last year, Taylor Farms donated $1m to Maga Inc, a Trump-affiliated Super Pac, according to financial records obtained by Wired.

Potential political interference was also concerning, making it more difficult to trust what’s coming from officials and companies, Jetelina said. “Trust is everything. And trust is not declared; it’s demonstrated.”

She pointed to Taco Bell, which was “incredibly cooperative” and worked quickly to pull potentially affected products and trace them back to the supplier, Jetelina said. “I was very impressed with how quickly they owned this and came out and communicated and acted,” which she contrasted with a “more uncooperative” Taylor Farms, which appears to be slow-walking the response. “And the question is why, and why isn’t there more pressure from the federal government?”

Mega-producers can meet a lot of demand for food, Sharfstein said. “But if there is a problem, that problem can be pretty widespread.”

With cyclospora, washing doesn’t really help that much, unlike E coli or salmonella. “So we are relying on the regulatory and public health system to protect us,” Sharfstein said.

“You could call it the explosive diarrhea rule,” he added. “When you’re not having explosive diarrhea, you don’t realize that the regulatory and public health systems are protecting you. When you do have explosive diarrhea, you’re like, ‘What’s going wrong? And we need to invest in systems to keep us from getting exposed to diarrhea.’”

title: Mamdani warning to wealthy New Yorkers about 'fair share' sparks online firestorm: 'Full blown communist'
excerpt: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's "pied-a-terre" wealth tax on luxury properties ignites a contentious debate, drawing strong criticism from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin and hedge fund manager Bill Ackm...
body_text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's "pied-a-terre" wealth tax on luxury properties ignites a contentious debate, drawing strong criticism from Citadel CEO Ken Griffin and hedge fund manager Bill Ackman.

New York City socialist mayor Zohran Mamdani is facing heat on social media after his post celebrating the state’s new pied-à-terre tax on New Yorkers with a second home.

"If you have a second home in New York City worth more than $5 million, check your mailbox when you’re back in the five boroughs — because you've got mail," Mamdani posted on X, touting the tax on specific second properties introduced by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul that he supported going into effect soon.

"Today, we sent notification letters to property owners, letting them know that our new pied-à-terre tax is coming soon," Mamdani continued. "The best city in the world deserves the best parks, libraries, and schools in the world. That's only possible when we all pay our fair share. "

As of Friday morning, Mamdani’s post had been viewed over 10 million times and conservatives on social media blasted the mayor and warned that the exodus of wealthy New Yorkers will only continue under this new plan.

HOCHUL CONFRONTED ON STUDY SHOWING MILLIONAIRE EXODUS IN NEW YORK CITY

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's video admitting that he lacks the legal authority to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu did little to ease Jewish leaders' concerns. (NYC Mayor's Office via YouTube/Handout via Reuters)

"Never elect a politician who: (1) sees your money as his slush fund, (2) loves Karl Marx, or (3) uses French words like ‘pied-à-terre’ to disguise new, confiscatory taxes he wants to impose to redistribute wealth," Republican Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT) posted on X.

"Socialism - Florida’s best real estate agent," Republican Sen. Ashley Moody (R-FL) posted on X.

"NYC’s pied-à-terre tax hasn’t even started and brokers already say owners are calling to sell," GOP strategist and attorney Mehek Cooke posted on X. "Empty units don’t tip [doormen] or pay supers. You’re not taxing the rich. You’re firing the working class that depended on them. "

"More incitement," Judicial Watch President Tom Fitton posted on X. "Communist @NYCMayor celebrates a confiscatory tax targeted at a select few. "

MAMDANI SETS INTERNET ABLAZE WITH VIDEO EXPLAINING CAVE ON PLAN TO ARREST NETANYAHU: 'WHAT A JOKE'

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul speaks about the excitement of seeing the Buffalo Bills in Western New York for the next 30 years during the ribbon cutting ceremony for the new Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park on June 23, 2026. (Shawn Dowd/Rochester Democrat and Chronicle / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

"What will the excuse be when literally nothing improves after all these tax increases?" New York City Republican Councilwoman Vickie Paladino posted on X. "Will they just demand even more, or will they tell us to ignore our own eyes as they insist they’ve actually fixed everything? Both? "

"The condescension towards the people who already pay a ton of property taxes to NYC," Washington Free Beacon investigative reporter Chuck Ross posted on X. "He thinks you're an immoral person and worthy of mockery if you have a second home. ‘when you're back in the five boroughs.’"

"That's only possible when we all pay our fair share,’ says the man who’s literally lived off of taxpayer dollars for years, produces nothing, and is concentrating the burdens on others—others who’ve contributed exponentially more to the city in both taxes and charitable contributions than he could possibly hope to contribute in 10 lifetimes, I might add," Manhattan Institute fellow Rafael Mangual posted on X.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks at a rally in New York alongside 1199SEIU members and immigration advocates after the Supreme Court ruled the Trump administration can revoke protections for Haitians and Syrians. (Lev Radin/Pacific Press/LightRocket via Getty Images)

"You can practically feel the glee emanating from this tweet so it's hilarious that people will still refuse to admit he's a full-blown communist," civil rights attorney David Pivtorak posted on X.

Mamdani’s support of the pied-à-terre tax on second homes worth more than $5 million has been a viral controversy for months and started when

In April, New York City Mayor Mamdani and Hochul unveiled the joint legislative proposal targeting luxury second homes worth $5 million or more. Known as a pied-à-terre tax, the annual surcharge is expected to generate an estimated $500 million from affluent out-of-state property owners.

Mamdani has previously said revenue from the tax would go toward initiatives such as free childcare, cleaner streets and safer neighborhoods.

Critics, including billionaire Ken Griffin whose luxury New York City home was featured in Mamdani's controversial video announcing the tax, argue the tax will only drive more wealthy New Yorkers out of the state and bring jobs and investments with them.

Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani's office for comment.

Fox Business's Kristen Altus contributed to this report

Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter at Fox News. Find him on Twitter @andymarkmiller and email tips to AndrewMark.Miller@Fox.com.
